50+-- In the final chaper of *Logical Foundations* (*Software Foundations*,
51+-- volume 1), we began applying the mathematical tools developed in the first
52+-- part of the course to studying the theory of a small programming language,
53+-- Imp.
54+
55+-- - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with an
56+--   *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that specifies the
57+--   *operational semantics* of programs.
58+
59+--   The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key features of
60+--   full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the fundamental
61+--   notion of mutable state and some common control structures.
62+
63+-- - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the sense
64+--   that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather than of
65+--   particular programs in the language. These included:
66+
67+--   - determinism of evaluation
68+
69+--   - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions (e.g.,
70+--     functional and relational definitions of arithmetic expression evaluation)
71+
72+--   - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
73+
74+--   - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of useful
75+--     program transformations
76+
77+--   - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the *Equiv* chapter).
78+
79+-- If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of tools
80+-- for defining and discussing programming languages and language features
81+-- that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work with, applied
82+-- to a set of key properties. All of these properties are things that
83+-- language designers, compiler writers, and users might care about knowing.
84+-- Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our understanding of the
85+-- programming languages we deal with that we might not consciously recognize
86+-- them as "theorems." But properties that seem intuitively obvious can
87+-- sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also subtly wrong!).
88+
89+-- We'll return to the theme of metatheoretic properties of whole languages
90+-- later in this volume when we discuss *types* and *type soundness*. In this
91+-- chapter, though, we turn to a different set of issues.
92+
93+-- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
94+-- simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
95+-- definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
96+-- particular specifications of their behavior.
97+
98+-- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
99+-- shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
100+-- constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used
101+-- to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs involving this
102+-- construct.
103+
104+-- Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject of
105+-- intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core of a
106+-- multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to specify
107+-- and verify real software systems.
108+
109+-- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
110+-- *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
111+-- proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications --
112+-- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors
113+-- the structure of the programs that they are about.
114+
115+-- Note to developers:
116+--     `HIDE: MRC'20: The terse version used to start with just an outline of
117+--     what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
118+--     The text above seems like a better intro.
119+--
120+--     MRC'20: this is the former terse intro.
121+--
122+--      What we've done so far:
123+--
124+--      - Formalized Imp
125+--           - identifiers and states
126+--           - abstract syntax trees
127+--           - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
128+--           - evaluation relation (for commands)
129+--
130+--      - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
131+--          - determinism of evaluation
132+--          - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
133+--            definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
134+--            arithmetic expression evaluation)
135+--          - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
136+--          - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
137+--          - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
138+--
139+--      We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
140+--        - Termination
141+--        - Nontermination
142+--        - Equivalence
143+--
144+--      Topic:
145+--        - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
146+--          correctness_ of programs in Imp
147+--
148+--      Goals:
149+--        - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
150+--        - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
151+--
152+--      Plan:
153+--        - specifications (assertions / Hoare triples)
154+--        - proof rules
155+--        - loop invariants
156+--        - decorated programs
157+--        - examples`
158+
159+-- ## Assertions
160+
161+open scoped MyGetElem
162+
163+-- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory --
164+-- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
165+
166+abbrev Assertion := State → Prop
167+
168+-- Note to developers:
169+--     HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the quiz/optional exercise
170+--     so that there would be some modeling of the kinds of answers we expect.
171+
172+-- For example,
173+
174+-- - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value of `X` is `3`,
175+-- - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
176+-- - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
177+
178+-- _Quiz:_
179+
180+-- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e., say which states
181+-- satisfy them)
182+
183+-- (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
184+
185+-- (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
186+
187+-- (C)
188+-- `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`
189+
190+-- ### Exercise (1 star): assertions ⭐
191+
192+-- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (or your favorite natural
193+-- language).
194+
195+namespace ExAssertions
196+def assertion1 : Assertion := fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]
197+def assertion2 : Assertion :=
198+  fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]
199+def assertion3 : Assertion :=
200+  fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧
201+            ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])
202+def assertion4 : Assertion :=
203+  fun st => st[Z] = max st[X] st[Y]
204+
205+end ExAssertions
206+
207+-- ### Notations for Assertions
208+
209+-- This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two reasons:
210+-- (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to begin with
211+-- `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that we ever use to
212+-- look up variables in assertions (we will almost never need to talk about
213+-- two different memory states at the same time). For discussing examples
214+-- informally, we'll adopt some simplifying conventions: we'll drop the
215+-- initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus,
216+-- instead of writing
217+
218+--   fun st => st[X] = m
219+
220+-- we'll write just
221+
222+--   {{ X = m }}.
223+
224+-- Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
225+-- assertion. We'll see more examples below.
226+
227+-- This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout the
228+-- Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like `X`,
229+-- `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`, `y`, `m`,
230+-- and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is why, when
231+-- translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with `st[X]` but leave
232+-- `m` alone.
233+
234+-- Note to developers (before next release):
235+--     RRand 2022: The coercion printing in recent updates is making the Hoare
236+--     logic statements we're aiming to prove essentially unreadable. If the
237+--     implicit coercions are too hard to deal with (I don't see why they
238+--     would be, given the number of coercion happening here and in Imp) I
239+--     would roll back to a previous version. I cannot read what's happening
240+--     in my Rocq buffer.
241+
242+-- Note to developers:
243+--     `HIDE: SAZ  2024: I'm confused by the above discussion.  Doesn't
244+--     [Add Printing Coercion Aexp_of_nat Aexp_of_aexp assert_of_Prop]
245+--     request Rocq to _show_ those coercions?  I've removed it.`
246+--
247+--     `HIDE: SAZ 2024:
248+--     From what I can tell, the reason the notations expand during
249+--     the proofs is that they're writen in such a way that they
250+--     inlude type annotations [(a : Aexp)] and explicit lambdas
251+--     [(fun st => a st + b st)], neither of which is stable under
252+--     simplification.  For example:
253+--
254+--      [(fun st =>
255+--         (fun st => (X:Aexp) st + (Y:Aexp) st) st +
256+--         (fun st => (Z:Aexp) st) st)]
257+--
258+--     Will print as [X + Y + Z] until simplification, at which point
259+--     we have [(fun st => st X + st Y + st Z)] but there is no notation
260+--     that covers this case.`
261+
262+-- The convention described above can be implemented with a little syntax
263+-- magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
264+-- `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts `Aexp`s,
265+-- numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear between the
266+-- `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an expression is
267+-- `Assertion`.
268+
269+-- There is no need to understand the details of how these notation hacks
270+-- work. (We barely understand some of it ourselves!)
271+
272+-- Note to developers:
273+--     HIDE: Make things easily unfoldable.
274+--
275+--     HIDE: MRC'20: Recording this here because it took a merry chase through
276+--     the Rocq manual to find it: this version of the `Arguments` command is
277+--     documented under `simpl`.
278+
279+-- Note to developers (One An  @meluge):
280+--     The Rocq source here issues `Arguments assert_of_Prop /.` (and likewise
281+--     for the other two lifting functions) so that `simpl` always unfolds
282+--     them, with this instructors note: "These `Arguments` commands tell Rocq
283+--     that these functions should always be unfolded during simplification
284+--     (by `simpl`)."
285+--
286+--     `SAZ 2024 - Why do we want these functions to simplify?
287+--     Ans: If [a : aexp] then in the assertion_scope [(X →ₜ a st; st)] and
288+--     [(X →ₜ aeval st a; st)] look different but are actually identical
289+--     thanks to the coercion [Aexp_of_aexp].`
290+--
291+--     Claude suggested `@[simp]`-tagged characterizing lemmas next to the
292+--     three lifting functions, a global simp attribute means every `simp`
293+--     unfolds applied occurrences. Is there a better way?
294+
295+-- Note to developers:
296+--     NOTATION: BCP 20: It probably makes sense now to put all these in a
297+--     custom grammar, so that we can really control how it looks and get rid
298+--     of things like ap.
299+--
300+--     `NOTATION: SAZ 2024: I have tried to implement the suggestion above.
301+--
302+--     There is now a custom entry [assn] for defining the syntax of
303+--     assertions.  Like the delimiters <{ }> used for Imp programs,
304+--     we now also have {{ }} delimiters for use with Assertions.
305+--
306+--     Inside that scope, the meaning of variables, nat literals,
307+--     propositions, etc. is "lifted" to take a state parameter.
308+--
309+--     The notation {{ #f x1 .. xn }} now "lifts" a normal function
310+--     that should be of type [nat -> .. -> nat -> T] so that each of
311+--     the inputs is treated as an [Aexp] and the state is threaded through.
312+--     (This replaces the need for [ap], [ap2], etc. throughout.)
313+--
314+--     The notation {{ $rocq_term }} now "quotes" a rocq term literally
315+--     without lifting.  Parentheses can be used as in {{ $(foo bar) }}.`
316+
317+-- Note to developers (Claude):
318+--     Delaborators for this grammar are defined in the *Printing Assertions*
319+--     section below (after assertion substitution, the last notation they
320+--     need to recognize). They cover the base chapter's forms -- triples,
321+--     `->>`, substitution, and lifted `Prop`s; not covered are the extension
322+--     modules' shadowed triples (each module defines its own `Com` and
323+--     `ValidHoareTriple`) and the `bassertion` coercion, which fall back to
324+--     raw display. An assertion applied to a state (after `intro st`) also
325+--     prints raw -- the same thing that happens in the Rocq development as
326+--     soon as `simpl` unfolds the notation.
327+
328+namespace Assertion
329+
330+section
331+open Lean Elab Term
332+
333+scoped syntax:max (name := assn) "assn(" ident "; " term ")" : term
334+scoped syntax "{{" term "}}" : term
335+
336+@[term_elab assn]
337+def assnElab : TermElab := fun stx type? => do
338+  match stx with
339+  | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
340+    let t ← elabTerm t none
341+    let ty ← Meta.inferType t
342+    dbg_trace ty
343+    -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
344+    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
345+      return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
346+        (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
347+        (mkConst ``String)
348+        (mkConst ``Nat)
349+        (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
350+          (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
351+          (mkConst ``String)
352+          (mkConst ``Nat))
353+        (← elabTerm st none) t
354+    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
355+      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
356+    else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then  -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
357+      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
358+    else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
359+      return t
360+    else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
361+      return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
362+    else
363+      return t
364+  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
365+
366+-- `: Assertion` guards that the resulting type is `State → Prop`.
367+macro_rules
368+  | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))
369+
370+macro_rules
371+  | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))
372+  | `(assn($st; $l = $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) = assn($st; $r))
373+  | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
374+  | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
375+  | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
376+  | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
377+  | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
378+  | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
379+  | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
380+  | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
381+  | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
382+  | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
383+  | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
384+  | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
385+  | `(assn($st; $f $a1)) => ``($f assn($st; $a1))
386+  | `(assn($st; $f $a1 $a2)) => ``($f assn($st; $a1) assn($st; $a2))
387+  -- | `(assn($st; $f $t*)) => ``($f ) -- TODO how to get arbitrary applications
388+end
389+
390+#check {{ 1 = 2 }}
391+#check {{ X = X }}
392+#check {{ X = 2 * X }} -- X is the constant "X" defined in Imp
393+#check_failure {{ X }} -- fails as expected
394+#check {{ True }}
395+
396+#check {{ fun st => st[X] = st[Y] }}
397+
398+variable (a : Aexp)
399+#check {{ X = a }}
400+
401+variable (b : Bexp)
402+#check {{ b }}
403+#check {{ ¬ b }}
404+#check {{ b ∧ b }}
405+
406+variable (P Q : Assertion)
407+#check {{ P ∧ Q }}
408+
409+end Assertion
410+
411+-- TODO OUTDATED One small limitation of this approach is that we don't have
412+-- an automatic way to coerce a function application that appears within an
413+-- assertion to make appropriate use of the state when its arguments should be
414+-- interpets as Imp arithmetic expressions. Instead, we introduce a notation
415+-- `#f e1 .. en` that stands for `fun st => f (e1 st) .. (en st)`, letting us
416+-- manually mark such function calls when they're needed as part of an
417+-- assertion.
418+
419+-- Note to developers:
420+--     NOTATION: This notation should come early so that later notations for
421+--     arithmetic expressions take precedence for printing. Otherwise
422+--     `{{ X + X }}` would print as `{{ #add X Y }}`.
423+
424+-- TODO OUTDATED Occasionally we need to "escape" a raw Lean function to
425+-- express a particularly complicated assertion. We can do that using a `~`
426+-- prefix, as in `{{ ~(raw_lean) }}` -- the same escape convention that the
427+-- `imp { … }` notation uses.
428+
429+-- For example, `{{ ~(fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0) }}` indicates an assertion
430+-- that every variable maps to `0` in the given state.
431+
432+-- Note to developers:
433+--     NOTATION: SAZ 2024: It is important that this custom notation be at a
434+--     level higher than 1 when added to the `constr` grammar because it
435+--     interacts with the "application" case of `com` and the notation for
436+--     Hoare triples. That grammar parses embedded function arguments at level
437+--     1. We never want `f {{P}}` to parse `{ P }` as an assertion when used
438+--     in a command. Instead we want `{{P}}` to "close" the Hoare triple.
439+--
440+--     `NOTATION: Note for Rocq custom grammar hackers.  From what I can tell, the
441+--     Rocq LL(1) parser does left-factorize the grammar, *however* it uses a very
442+--     strict notion of what counts as "equal" for the purposes of the factorization.
443+--     In particular, a grammar entry might have a level,
444+--     as in [e custom assn at level 99] in the notation below.  Leaving out the
445+--     "at level 99" is *semantically equivalent*, because the [assn] grammar starts
446+--     at that level, but omitting it will not work because the grammar for
447+--     Hoare triples below includes "at level 99" -- the [LEVEL "99"] part of the
448+--     grammar counts for factorization.
449+--
450+--     The upshot is that means that this notation and the Hoare triple notation
451+--     (which overlaps with [{{ _ }}]) must be changed in tandem and use identical
452+--     level specifications.`
453+
454+-- ### Example Assertions
455+
456+-- Here are some example assertions that take advantage of this new notation.
457+
458+namespace ExamplePrettyAssertions
459+open scoped Assertion
460+
461+def assertion1 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 }}
462+def assertion2 : Assertion := {{ True }}
463+def assertion3 : Assertion := {{ False }}
464+def assertion4 : Assertion := {{ True ∨ False }}
465+def assertion5 : Assertion := {{ X ≤ Y }}
466+def assertion6 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 ∨ X ≤ Y }}
467+def assertion7 : Assertion := {{ Z = (max X Y) }}
468+def assertion8 : Assertion := {{ Z * Z ≤ X
469+                                 ∧ ¬ (((Nat.succ Z) * (Nat.succ Z)) ≤ X) }}
470+def assertion9 : Assertion := {{ Nat.add X Y > max Y X }}
471+
472+/--
473+info: def ExamplePrettyAssertions.assertion8 : Assertion :=
474+fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬st[Z].succ * st[Z].succ ≤ st[X]
475+-/
476+#guard_msgs in
477+#print assertion8
478+
479+end ExamplePrettyAssertions

481+-- ### Assertion Implication
482+
483+-- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
484+-- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
485+
486+def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
487+  ∀ st, P st → Q st
488+
489+-- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
490+-- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
491+
492+notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
493+
494+theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
495+
496+-- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
497+
498+notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
499+
500+-- Note to developers (Claude):
501+--     The Rocq source puts these notations in a `hoare_spec_scope`, with a
502+--     book comment explaining that "the `hoare_spec_scope` annotation tells
503+--     Rocq that this notation is not global but is intended to be used in
504+--     particular contexts." Lean has no notation scopes, so the notations are
505+--     simply global and that paragraph is omitted.
506+
507+-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
508+
509+-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
510+-- command. The standard notation is
511+
512+--   {P} c {Q}
513+
514+-- meaning:
515+
516+-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
517+-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
518+-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
519+
520+-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
521+-- *postcondition*.
522+
523+-- Because single braces are already used for other things in Lean, we'll
524+-- write Hoare triples with double braces:
525+
526+--   {{P}} c {{Q}}
527+
528+-- For example,
529+
530+-- - The Hoare triple
531+
532+--   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
533+
534+-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
535+-- a state in which `X = 1`.
536+
537+-- - On the other hand,
538+
539+--   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
540+
541+-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
542+-- `{{X = m}} X :=
543+-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
544+-- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
545+-- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
546+
547+-- _Quiz:_
548+
549+-- Paraphrase the following in English.
550+
551+--   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
552+
553+--   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
554+
555+--   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
556+
557+--   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
558+
559+--   5) ∀ m,
560+--        {{X = m}}
561+--        c
562+--        {{Y = real_fact m}}
563+
564+--   6) ∀ m,
565+--        {{X = m}}
566+--        c
567+--        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
568+
569+-- _Quiz:_
570+
571+-- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
572+-- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
573+
574+--   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
575+
576+-- (A) Yes
577+
578+-- (B) No
579+
580+-- _Quiz:_
581+
582+-- What about this one?
583+
584+--   {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
585+
586+-- (A) Yes
587+
588+-- (B) No
589+
590+-- _Quiz:_
591+
592+-- What about this one?
593+
594+--   {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
595+
596+-- (A) Yes
597+
598+-- (B) No
599+
600+-- _Quiz:_
601+
602+-- What about this one?
603+
604+--   {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
605+
606+-- (A) Yes
607+
608+-- (B) No
609+
610+-- _Quiz:_
611+
612+-- What about this one?
613+
614+--   {{True}} skip {{False}}
615+
616+-- (A) Yes
617+
618+-- (B) No
619+
620+-- _Quiz:_
621+
622+-- What about this one?
623+
624+--   {{False}} skip {{True}}
625+
626+-- (A) Yes
627+
628+-- (B) No
629+
630+-- _Quiz:_
631+
632+-- What about this one?
633+
634+--   {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
635+
636+-- (A) Yes
637+
638+-- (B) No
639+
640+-- _Quiz:_
641+
642+-- This one?
643+
644+--   {{X = 0}}
645+--     while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
646+--   {{X = 1}}
647+
648+-- (A) Yes
649+
650+-- (B) No
651+
652+-- _Quiz:_
653+
654+-- This one?
655+
656+--   {{X = 1}}
657+--     while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
658+--   {{X = 100}}
659+
660+-- (A) Yes
661+
662+-- (B) No
663+
664+-- ### Exercise (1 star): valid_triples ⭐
665+
666+-- Which of the following Hoare triples are *valid* -- i.e., the claimed
667+-- relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` is true?
668+
669+--   1) {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
670+
671+--   2) {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
672+
673+--   3) {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
674+
675+--   4) {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
676+
677+--   5) {{True}} skip {{False}}
678+
679+--   6) {{False}} skip {{True}}
680+
681+--   7) {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
682+
683+--   8) {{X = 0}}
684+--       while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
685+--     {{X = 1}}
686+
687+--   9) {{X = 1}}
688+--       while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
689+--     {{X = 100}}
690+
691+-- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
692+
693+-- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
694+
695+def ValidHoareTriple
696+    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
697+  ∀ st st',
698+    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
699+    P st →
700+    Q st'
701+
702+-- Note to developers:
703+--     `NOTATION: SAZ 2024 One trickiness of these notations is that we
704+--     want the [com] and [assn] grammars to be "open", so that they can
705+--     include expressions parsed by the full [constr] grammar of Rocq.
706+--     However, then there is a conflict of precedence of the
707+--     "application" cases:
708+--
709+--     The example " {{ True }} X := 0 {{ False }} " does not parse as
710+--     intended because the [com] grammar includes the capability of
711+--     parsing the (ill-typed) term "0 {{ False }}".
712+--
713+--     This means that the "application" for [com] should disallow
714+--     arguments at the level at which the [assn] grammar is included
715+--     in constr.  The upshot is that this notation should be included
716+--     in the grammar at the *same* level as the assertion notation
717+--     [{{ P }}], which is 2.`
718+
719+-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
720+-- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
721+-- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
722+-- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
723+
724+open scoped Assertion
725+
726+namespace ValidHoareTriple
727+
728+/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
729+scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
730+
731+macro_rules
732+  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
733+      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
734+
735+end ValidHoareTriple
736+
737+section
738+open scoped ValidHoareTriple
739+

741+--     `HIDE: AAA: If I try to set the notation as {P} c {Q}, I get the
742+--     following error:
743+--
744+--       Error: A notation must include at least one symbol.
745+--
746+--     Maybe we could use other braces? For instance, I tried it with [P]
747+--     c [Q] and it seems to work (although I don't know how that would
748+--     affect the rest of the book).
749+--
750+--     BCP: Let's try with the "squashed" double braces for a while and
751+--     see if we like it.
752+--
753+--     P.S.
754+--     This works:
755+--        Notation "{ x }" := (x) (at level 0, x at level 99).
756+--     But this doesn't:
757+--        Notation "{ P }  c  { Q }" :=
758+--          (ValidHoareTriple P c Q)
759+--          (at level 0, P at level 99, c at level 99, Q at level 99)
760+--        : hoare_spec_scope.
761+--     Why??`
762+
763+-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_post_true ⭐
764+
765+-- Prove that if `Q` holds in every state, then any triple with `Q` as its
766+-- postcondition is valid.
767+
768+theorem hoare_post_true (P Q : Assertion) (c : Com) (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
769+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
770+  sorry
771+
772+-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false ⭐
773+
774+-- Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with `P` as its
775+-- precondition is valid.
776+
777+theorem hoare_pre_false (P Q : Assertion) (c : Com) (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
778+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
779+  sorry
780+
781+-- ## Proof Rules
782+
783+-- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
784+-- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
785+-- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
786+-- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
787+-- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
788+-- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
789+-- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
790+-- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
791+-- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
792+
793+-- ### Skip
794+
795+-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
796+
797+--   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
798+--   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
799+
800+theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
801+    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
802+  intro st st' h hp
803+  inversion h
804+  assumption
805+
806+-- ### Sequencing
807+
808+-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
809+-- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
810+-- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
811+-- where `R` holds:
812+
813+--    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
814+--    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
815+--   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
816+--   {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
817+
818+theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
819+    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
820+    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{ R }} := by
821+  intro st st' h12 pre
822+  inversion h12 with
823+  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
824+    exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
825+
826+-- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
827+-- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
828+-- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
829+-- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
830+-- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
831+-- through commands until we reach the beginning.
832+
833+-- ### Assignment
834+
835+-- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
836+-- rules. Here's how it works.
837+
838+-- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
839+
840+--   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
841+
842+-- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
843+-- could the precondition be?
844+
845+-- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
846+-- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
847+
848+--   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
849+
850+-- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
851+-- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
852+-- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
853+-- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
854+-- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
855+
856+-- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
857+
858+--   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
859+
860+-- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
861+-- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
862+
863+--   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
864+
865+-- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
866+-- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
867+-- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
868+-- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
869+-- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
870+-- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
871+-- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
872+
873+-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
874+-- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
875+-- expression `a`:
876+
877+--   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
878+
879+-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
880+-- replaced by `a`.
881+
882+-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
883+-- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
884+
885+-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
886+
887+--   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
888+
889+-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
890+-- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
891+-- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
892+-- for every occurrence of `X`.
893+
894+-- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
895+-- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
896+-- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
897+-- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
898+
899+-- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
900+-- We'll do that later in some exercises.
901+
902+-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
903+
904+--   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
905+--     X := X + 1
906+--   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
907+
908+--   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
909+--     X := 3
910+--   {{ X = 3 }}
911+
912+--   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
913+--     X := 3
914+--   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
915+
916+-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
917+-- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
918+-- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.sub`.
919+
920+-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
921+-- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
922+-- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
923+
924+-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
925+-- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
926+-- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
927+-- directly "edit" its text.
928+
929+-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
930+-- state, defined as follows:
931+
932+def Assertion.sub (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
933+  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
934+
935+-- Note to developers (before next release):
936+--     This concrete syntax is hard to read in comments because of all the
937+--     square brackets. Something like `P with X ↦ a` would be much better. I
938+--     guess the same will apply to the lambda-calculus chapters... BCP 25: I
939+--     still think this is a good idea, and I had a quick go at implementing
940+--     it, but did not succeed yet.
941+
942+-- TODO Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)
943+
944+/-- Assertion substitution: `P [X ↦ a]` -/
945+syntax:100 term:100 " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
946+
947+macro_rules
948+  | `($P [$x ↦ $a]) => `(Assertion.sub $x (aexp { $a }) $P)
949+  -- | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a])) => ``(assn($st; $P) [$x ↦ $a]) -- maybe we could push substitutions inside
950+
951+-- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
952+
953+--   P [ X ↦ a ]
954+
955+#check (fun st => Assertion.sub X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
956+#check {{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]
957+#check (∀ st, ({{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]) st)
958+
959+-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
960+-- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
961+-- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
962+
963+-- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
964+-- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
965+-- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
966+
967+--   fun st =>
968+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
969+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
970+
971+-- which simplifies to
972+
973+--   fun st =>
974+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
975+--     (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
976+
977+-- and further simplifies to
978+
979+--   fun st =>
980+--     ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
981+
982+-- and finally to
983+
984+--   fun st =>
985+--     3 ≤ 5.
986+
987+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
988+-- expected).
989+
990+-- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
991+-- X + 1]`.
992+-- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
993+
994+--   fun st =>
995+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
996+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
997+
998+-- which simplifies to
999+
1000+--   fun st =>
1001+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
1002+
1003+-- and further simplifies to
1004+
1005+--   fun st =>
1006+--     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1007+
1008+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.
1009+
1010+-- We can demonstrate formally that we have captured intuitive meaning of
1011+-- "assertion subsitution" by proving some example logical equivalences:
1012+
1013+namespace ExampleAssertionSub
1014+example :
1015+    {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ 3] <<->> {{ 3 ≤ 5 }} := by
1016+  constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
1017+
1018+example :
1019+    {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ X + 1] <<->> {{ (X + 1) ≤ 5 }} := by
1020+  constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
1021+
1022+end ExampleAssertionSub
1023+
1024+-- ### Printing Assertions
1025+
1026+-- As in the Imp chapter, the assertion notations above are *input* only: Lean
1027+-- reads `{{ X ≤ 5 }}` but still prints the underlying function. The
1028+-- delaborators below close the loop for the common cases: Hoare triples,
1029+-- `->>` implications, and assertion substitutions are printed back in their
1030+-- concrete notation, and an assertion Lean cannot rebuild falls back to the
1031+-- `~` escape (or, ultimately, to the raw term). As before, there is no need
1032+-- to understand the details, and everything can be switched off with
1033+-- `set_option pp.notation false`.
1034+

1238+
1239+-- Now, using the substitution operation we've just defined, we can give the
1240+-- precise proof rule for assignment:
1241+
1242+--   ---------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1243+--   {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X := a {{Q}}
1244+
1245+-- We can prove formally that this rule is indeed valid.
1246+
1247+theorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
1248+    {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}  x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by
1249+  intro st st' hE hQ
1250+  inversion hE with
1251+  | asgn n h =>
1252+    subst h
1253+    exact hQ
1254+
1255+-- Here's a first formal proof of a Hoare triple using this rule.
1256+
1257+theorem assertion_sub_example :
1258+    {{ {{ X < 5 }} [X ↦ X + 1] }}
1259+      X := X + 1;
1260+    {{ X < 5 }} := by
1261+  apply hoare_asgn
1262+
1263+-- Of course, we'd probably prefer to work with this simpler triple:
1264+
1265+--   {{X < 4}} X := X + 1 {{X < 5}}
1266+
1267+-- We will see how to do so in the next section.
1268+
1269+-- Several proofs below use the facts about total-map updates proved in the
1270+-- *Typeclasses* chapter -- `TotalMap.update_eq`, `TotalMap.update_neq`,
1271+-- `TotalMap.update_shadow`, `TotalMap.update_same`, and
1272+-- `TotalMap.update_permute`. Make sure you understand their statements.
1273+
1274+-- Complete these Hoare triples by providing an appropriate precondition using
1275+-- `exists`, then prove then with `apply
1276+-- hoare_asgn`. If you find that tactic
1277+-- doesn't suffice, double check that you have completed the triple properly.
1278+
1279+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_examples1 ⭐⭐
1280+
1281+theorem hoare_asgn_examples1 :
1282+    ∃ P : Assertion,
1283+      {{ P }}
1284+        X := 2 * X;
1285+      {{ X ≤ 10 }} := by
1286+  sorry
1287+
1288+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_examples2 ⭐⭐
1289+
1290+theorem hoare_asgn_examples2 :
1291+    ∃ P : Assertion,
1292+      {{ P }}
1293+        X := 3;
1294+      {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }} := by
1295+  sorry
1296+
1297+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_wrong ⭐⭐
1298+
1299+-- The assignment rule looks backward to almost everyone the first time they
1300+-- see it. If it still seems puzzling to you, it may help to think a little
1301+-- about alternative "forward" rules. Here is a seemingly natural one:
1302+
1303+--   ------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_wrong)
1304+--   {{ True }} X := a {{ X = a }}
1305+
1306+-- Give a counterexample showing that this rule is incorrect and use it to
1307+-- complete the proof below, showing that it is really a counterexample.
1308+-- (Hint: The rule universally quantifies over the arithmetic expression `a`,
1309+-- so your counterexample needs to exhibit an `a` for which the rule doesn't
1310+-- work.)
1311+
1312+theorem hoare_asgn_wrong : ∃ a : Aexp,
1313+    ¬ {{ True }} X := ~a; {{ X = a }} := by
1314+  sorry
1315+
1316+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1317+
1318+-- By using a *parameter* `m` (a Lean number) to remember the original value
1319+-- of `X` we can define a Hoare rule for assignment that does, intuitively,
1320+-- "work forwards" rather than backwards.
1321+
1322+--   ------------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd)
1323+--   {{fun st => P st ∧ st[X] = m}}
1324+--     X := a
1325+--   {{fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧ st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1326+
1327+-- Note that we need to write out the postcondition in "desugared" form,
1328+-- because it needs to talk about two different states: we use the original
1329+-- value of `X` to reconstruct the state `st'` before the assignment took
1330+-- place. (Also note that this rule is more complicated than `hoare_asgn`!)
1331+
1332+-- Prove that this rule is correct.
1333+
1334+-- Note to developers:
1335+--     HIDE: BCP 21: Could we make the precondition use compact notation, at
1336+--     least?
1337+--
1338+--     HIDE: SAZ 2024 - this version of the syntax does let us use the compact
1339+--     notation for the precondition, but it comes at the cost of having to
1340+--     "escape" the function in the postcondition.
1341+
1342+theorem hoare_asgn_fwd (m : Nat) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) :
1343+    {{ P ∧ X = m }}
1344+      X := ~a;
1345+    {{ fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st)
1346+         ∧ st[X] = a.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) }} := by
1347+  sorry
1348+
1349+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd_exists (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1350+
1351+-- Another way to define a forward rule for assignment is to existentially
1352+-- quantify over the previous value of the assigned variable. Prove that it is
1353+-- correct.
1354+
1355+--   ------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd_exists)
1356+--   {{fun st => P st}}
1357+--     X := a
1358+--   {{fun st => ∃ m, P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧
1359+--                  st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1360+
1361+theorem hoare_asgn_fwd_exists (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) :
1362+    {{ P }}
1363+      X := ~a;
1364+    {{ fun st => ∃ m, P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧
1365+         st[X] = a.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) }} := by
1366+  sorry
1367+
1368+-- ### Consequence
1369+
1370+-- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare rules
1371+-- won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at hand -- they
1372+-- may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails
1373+-- to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually may be
1374+-- logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
1375+-- what we need.
1376+
1377+-- For instance,
1378+
1379+--   {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1380+
1381+-- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1382+
1383+--   {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1384+
1385+-- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of `hoare_asgn`
1386+-- because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal
1387+-- assertions.
1388+
1389+-- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid, then
1390+-- the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this observation with
1391+-- the following rule:
1392+
1393+--      {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1394+--        P <<->> P'
1395+--   ---------------------
1396+--      {{P}} c {{Q}}
1397+
1398+-- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that strengthening
1399+-- the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a valid triple always
1400+-- produces another valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules
1401+-- of Consequence*.
1402+
1403+--          {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1404+--             P ->> P'
1405+--   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1406+--          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1407+
1408+--          {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1409+--            Q' ->> Q
1410+--   -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1411+--          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1412+
1413+-- Here are the formal versions:
1414+
1415+theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1416+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1417+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1418+  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1419+  intro st st' heval hpre
1420+  apply hhoare st st'
1421+  · assumption
1422+  · apply himp
1423+    assumption
1424+
1425+theorem hoare_consequence_post (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1426+    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1427+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1428+  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1429+  intro st st' heval hpre
1430+  apply himp
1431+  apply hhoare st st'
1432+  · assumption
1433+  · assumption
1434+
1435+-- For example, we can use the first consequence rule like this:
1436+
1437+--   {{ True }} ->>
1438+--   {{ (X = 1) [X ↦ 1] }}
1439+--     X := 1
1440+--   {{ X = 1 }}
1441+
1442+-- Or, formally...
1443+
1444+theorem hoare_asgn_example1 :
1445+    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1446+  all_goals
1447+    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1448+    · apply hoare_asgn
1449+    · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1450+      intro st _
1451+      rfl
1452+
1453+-- We can also use it to prove the example mentioned earlier.
1454+
1455+--   {{ X < 4 }} ->>
1456+--   {{ (X < 5)[X ↦ X + 1] }}
1457+--     X := X + 1
1458+--   {{ X < 5 }}
1459+
1460+-- Or, formally ...
1461+
1462+theorem assertion_sub_example2 :
1463+    {{X < 4}}
1464+      X := X + 1;
1465+    {{X < 5}} := by
1466+  all_goals
1467+    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1468+    · apply hoare_asgn
1469+    · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1470+      intro st h
1471+      simp [TotalMap.update_eq] at *
1472+      lia
1473+
1474+-- Finally, here is a combined rule of consequence that allows us to vary both
1475+-- the precondition and the postcondition.
1476+
1477+--          {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1478+--             P ->> P'
1479+--             Q' ->> Q
1480+--   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
1481+--          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1482+
1483+theorem hoare_consequence (P P' Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1484+    (htriple : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :
1485+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1486+  apply hoare_consequence_pre (P' := P')
1487+  · apply hoare_consequence_post (Q' := Q')
1488+    · assumption
1489+    · assumption
1490+  · assumption
1491+
1492+-- ### Automation
1493+
1494+-- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples can be
1495+-- streamlined using the automation techniques that we introduced in the
1496+-- *Automation* chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1497+
1498+-- Recall that the `simp` tactic can be told to unfold definitions as part of
1499+-- its simplifications. The definitions we keep needing to unfold in this
1500+-- chapter are `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, `Assertion.sub`, the
1501+-- lifting functions `Assertion.ofProp`, `Aexp'.ofNat`, and `Aexp'.ofAexp`,
1502+-- and the total-map operations. We'll pass these to `simp` explicitly below
1503+-- (and shortly package the recipe up as a tactic of our own).
1504+
1505+-- Note to developers (Claude):
1506+--     The Rocq source here registers
1507+--     `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1508+--     t_update : core` for `auto`.
1509+--     That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the `Arguments /.` commands,
1510+--     it does not affect `simpl`), so its Lean counterpart is the
1511+--     `assertion_auto` tactic's simp list below -- not global `@[simp]`
1512+--     lemmas as for the notation wrappers, whose folded names carry no
1513+--     meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.sub` do.
1514+
1515+-- The proof of `hoare_consequence_pre`, repeated below, looks like an
1516+-- opportune place for automation, because all it does is `unfold`, `intro`,
1517+-- and `apply`. (It uses `assumption`, too, but that's just application of a
1518+-- hypothesis.)
1519+
1520+theorem hoare_consequence_pre' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1521+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1522+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1523+  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1524+  intro st st' heval hpre
1525+  apply hhoare st st'
1526+  · assumption
1527+  · apply himp
1528+    assumption
1529+
1530+-- Notice that this proof passes the states `st` and `st'` to `apply
1531+-- hhoare`
1532+-- explicitly. We didn't actually need to: when an argument of the applied
1533+-- theorem is not determined by the goal, `apply` introduces a *metavariable*
1534+-- `?st` as a placeholder and lets a later step of the proof determine it.
1535+-- Here, `assumption` instantiates `?st` with `st` when it discovers `st` in
1536+-- the assumption `heval`. Using `apply` this way is like telling Lean, "Be
1537+-- patient: The missing part is going to be filled in later in the proof."
1538+
1539+theorem hoare_consequence_pre''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1540+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1541+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1542+  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1543+  intro st st' heval hpre
1544+  apply hhoare
1545+  · assumption
1546+  · apply himp
1547+    assumption
1548+
1549+-- Since the remaining steps just apply hypotheses to each other, the entire
1550+-- proof can actually be compressed into a single line, by writing the term
1551+-- that `exact`ly proves the conclusion.
1552+
1553+theorem hoare_consequence_pre'''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1554+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1555+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1556+  intro st st' heval hpre
1557+  exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
1558+
1559+-- Of course, it's hard to write such a one-liner without having gone through
1560+-- the original proof of `hoare_consequence_pre` to see the steps it used. But
1561+-- now that we know the shape of the argument, it's a good bet that the same
1562+-- trick will also work for `hoare_consequence_post`.
1563+
1564+theorem hoare_consequence_post' (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1565+    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1566+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1567+  intro st st' heval hpre
1568+  exact himp st' (hhoare st st' heval hpre)
1569+
1570+-- We can also use a metavariable to streamline a proof
1571+-- (`hoare_asgn_example1`), that we did earlier as an example of using the
1572+-- consequence rule:
1573+
1574+theorem hoare_asgn_example1' :
1575+    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1576+  apply hoare_consequence_pre  -- no need to state an assertion
1577+  · apply hoare_asgn
1578+  · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1579+    intro st _
1580+    rfl
1581+
1582+-- The final bullet of that proof also looks like a candidate for automation.
1583+
1584+theorem hoare_asgn_example1'' :
1585+    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1586+  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1587+  · apply hoare_asgn
1588+  · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, TotalMap.update_eq]
1589+
1590+-- Now we have quite a nice proof script: it simply identifies the Hoare rules
1591+-- that need to be used and leaves the remaining low-level details up to Lean
1592+-- to figure out.
1593+
1594+-- By now it might be apparent that the *entire* proof could be automated by a
1595+-- more ambitious tactic that also knew about the Hoare rules themselves. We
1596+-- won't build one in this chapter, so that we can get a better understanding
1597+-- of when and how the Hoare rules are used. In the next chapter, *Hoare2*,
1598+-- we'll dive deeper into automating entire proofs of Hoare triples.
1599+
1600+-- The other example of using consequence that we did earlier,
1601+-- `hoare_asgn_example2`, requires a little more work to automate. `simp`
1602+-- simplifies the assertion implication in the final bullet, but cannot finish
1603+-- it: the leftover goal is arithmetic, so it needs `lia`.
1604+
1605+theorem assertion_sub_example2' :
1606+    {{X < 4}}
1607+      X := X + 1;
1608+    {{X < 5}} := by
1609+  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1610+  · apply hoare_asgn
1611+  · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, TotalMap.update_eq]  -- an arithmetic goal remains
1612+    lia
1613+
1614+-- Let's introduce our own tactic to handle both that bullet and the bullet
1615+-- from example 1. A `macro` declaration gives a name to a canned sequence of
1616+-- tactics:
1617+
1618+/-- Prove routine facts about assertions: unfold the Hoare-logic
1619+definitions and lifting functions, simplify, and finish any leftover
1620+arithmetic with `lia`. -/
1621+macro "assertion_auto" : tactic =>
1622+  `(tactic| (intros
1623+             <;> try (simp [assertImplies_def, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
1624+                            TotalMap.update, TotalMap.getElem_def,
1625+                            W, X, Y, Z] at *)
1626+             <;> try lia))
1627+
1628+theorem assertion_sub_example2'' :
1629+    {{X < 4}}
1630+      X := X + 1;
1631+    {{X < 5}} := by
1632+  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1633+  · apply hoare_asgn
1634+  · assertion_auto
1635+
1636+theorem hoare_asgn_example1''' :
1637+    {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1638+  apply hoare_consequence_pre
1639+  · apply hoare_asgn
1640+  · assertion_auto
1641+
1642+-- Again, we have quite a nice proof script. All the low-level details of
1643+-- proofs about assertions have been taken care of automatically. Of course,
1644+-- `assertion_auto` isn't able to prove everything we could possibly want to
1645+-- know about assertions -- there's no magic here! But it's pretty good.
1646+
1647+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_examples_2 ⭐⭐
1648+
1649+-- Prove these triples. Try to make your proof scripts nicely automated by
1650+-- following the examples above.
1651+
1652+theorem assertion_sub_ex1' :
1653+    {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1654+      X := 2 * X;
1655+    {{ X ≤ 10 }} := by
1656+  sorry
1657+
1658+theorem assertion_sub_ex2' :
1659+    {{ 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5 }}
1660+      X := 3;
1661+    {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }} := by
1662+  sorry
1663+
1664+-- ### Sequencing + Assignment
1665+
1666+-- Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and assignment.
1667+-- Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with `hoare_consequence_pre` and
1668+-- `apply`'s metavariables.
1669+
1670+theorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1671+    {{a = n}}
1672+      X := ~a;
1673+      skip;
1674+    {{X = n}} := by
1675+  apply hoare_seq
1676+  · -- right part of seq
1677+    apply hoare_skip
1678+  · -- left part of seq
1679+    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1680+    · apply hoare_asgn
1681+    · assertion_auto
1682+
1683+-- Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the sequencing rule is
1684+-- as a "decorated program" where the intermediate assertion `Q` is written
1685+-- between `c1` and `c2`:
1686+
1687+--            {{ a = n }}
1688+--   X := a
1689+--            {{ X = n }};    <--- decoration for Q
1690+--   skip
1691+--            {{ X = n }}
1692+
1693+-- We'll come back to the idea of decorated programs in much more detail in
1694+-- the next chapter.
1695+
1696+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_example4 ⭐⭐
1697+
1698+-- Translate this "decorated program" into a formal proof:
1699+
1700+--                  {{ True }} ->>
1701+--                  {{ 1 = 1 }}
1702+--   X := 1
1703+--                  {{ X = 1 }} ->>
1704+--                  {{ X = 1 ∧ 2 = 2 }};
1705+--   Y := 2
1706+--                  {{ X = 1 ∧ Y = 2 }}
1707+
1708+-- Note the use of "`->>`" decorations, each marking a use of
1709+-- `hoare_consequence_pre`.
1710+
1711+-- We've started you off by providing a use of `hoare_seq` that explicitly
1712+-- identifies `X = 1` as the intermediate assertion.
1713+
1714+theorem hoare_asgn_example4 :
1715+    {{ True }}
1716+      X := 1;
1717+      Y := 2;
1718+    {{ X = 1 ∧ Y = 2 }} := by
1719+  apply hoare_seq (Q := {{ X = 1 }})
1720+  · -- right part of seq
1721+    sorry
1722+  · -- left part of seq
1723+    sorry
1724+
1725+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): swap_exercise ⭐⭐⭐
1726+
1727+-- Write an Imp program `c` that swaps the values of `X` and `Y` and show that
1728+-- it satisfies the following specification:
1729+
1730+--   {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
1731+
1732+-- Your proof should not need to use `unfold ValidHoareTriple`.
1733+
1734+-- Hints:
1735+
1736+-- - Remember that Imp commands need to be enclosed in `imp { … }` brackets.
1737+
1738+-- - Remember that the assignment rule works best when it's applied "back to
1739+--   front," from the postcondition to the precondition. So your proof will want
1740+--   to start at the end and work back to the beginning of your program.
1741+
1742+-- - Remember that `apply` is your friend.)
1743+
1744+-- Note to developers:
1745+--     `HIDE: CH: Here goes:
1746+--     [[
1747+--       {{ X ≤ Y }}
1748+--         Z := X
1749+--                 {{ Z ≤ Y }};
1750+--         X := Y
1751+--                 {{ Z ≤ X }};
1752+--         Y := Z
1753+--       {{ Y ≤ X }}
1754+--     ]]
1755+--        The _only_ catch is that one needs to do it backwards, since that's
1756+--        how the hoare_asgn rule is defined.
1757+--        Maybe move this decorated program to the decorated programs
1758+--        section, since it's a good warm-up exercise.`
1759+
1760+def swap_program : Com :=
1761+  sorry
1762+
1763+theorem swap_exercise :
1764+    {{X ≤ Y}}
1765+      ~swap_program
1766+    {{Y ≤ X}} := by
1767+  sorry

1769+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): invalid_triple (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1770+
1771+-- Show that
1772+
1773+--   {{ a = n }} X := 3; Y := a {{ Y = n }}
1774+
1775+-- is not a valid Hoare triple for some choices of `a` and `n`.
1776+
1777+-- Conceptual hint: Invent a particular `a` and `n` for which the triple in
1778+-- invalid, then use those to complete the proof.
1779+
1780+-- Technical hint: Hypothesis `h` below begins `∀ a n, ...`. You'll want to
1781+-- instantiate that with the particular `a` and `n` you've invented. You can
1782+-- do that with `have` and `apply`, but you may remember (from the
1783+-- *Automation* chapter of Logical Foundations) that Lean offers an even
1784+-- easier tactic: `specialize`. If you write
1785+
1786+--   specialize h your_a your_n
1787+
1788+-- the hypothesis will be instantiated on `your_a` and `your_n`.
1789+
1790+-- Having chosen your `a` and `n`, proceed as follows:
1791+
1792+-- - Use the (assumed) validity of the given hoare triple to derive a state
1793+--   `st'` in which `Y` has some value `y1`
1794+
1795+-- - Use the evaluation rules (`Com.EvalR.seq` and `Com.EvalR.asgn`) to show
1796+--   that `Y` has a *different* value `y2` in the same final state `st'`
1797+
1798+-- - Since `y1` and `y2` are both equal to `st'[Y]`, they are equal to each
1799+--   other. But we chose them to be different, so this is a contradiction, which
1800+--   finishes the proof.
1801+
1802+theorem invalid_triple : ¬ ∀ (a : Aexp) (n : Nat),
1803+    {{ a = n }}
1804+      X := 3; Y := ~a;
1805+    {{ Y = n }} := by
1806+  unfold ValidHoareTriple
1807+  intro h
1808+  sorry
1809+
1810+-- ### Conditionals
1811+
1812+-- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1813+
1814+-- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of the
1815+-- branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be tempted
1816+-- to write:
1817+
1818+--           {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1819+--           {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1820+--   ---------------------------------
1821+--   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1822+
1823+-- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot show
1824+
1825+--   {{ True }}
1826+--     if X = 0
1827+--       then Y := 2
1828+--       else Y := X + 1
1829+--     end
1830+--   {{ X ≤ Y }}
1831+
1832+-- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1833+-- assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1834+
1835+-- Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch, we
1836+-- know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the "else"
1837+-- branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information available
1838+-- in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work with when
1839+-- reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the reasons why they
1840+-- establish the postcondition `Q`).
1841+
1842+--   {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1843+--   {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1844+--   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1845+--   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1846+
1847+-- TODO OUTDATED To interpret this rule formally, we need to do a little work.
1848+-- Strictly speaking, the assertion we've written, `P ∧ b`, is the conjunction
1849+-- of an assertion and a boolean expression -- i.e., it doesn't typecheck. To
1850+-- fix this, we need a way of formally "lifting" any bexp `b` to an assertion.
1851+-- We'll write `bassertion b` for the assertion "the boolean expression `b`
1852+-- evaluates to `true` (in the given state)."
1853+
1854+def bassertion (b : Bexp) : Assertion := {{ b }} -- NOTE xhalo32: we don't need this IMO
1855+
1856+@[simp] theorem bassertion_apply (b : Bexp) (st : State) :
1857+    bassertion b st = (b.eval st = true) := rfl
1858+
1859+instance : Coe Bexp Assertion := ⟨bassertion⟩
1860+
1861+-- A useful fact about `bassertion`:
1862+
1863+-- Note to developers (before next release):
1864+--     `Robert Rand: This isn't an identity but that's because
1865+--     we're using [~(bassertion b st)] in our triples, instead of a more
1866+--     direct/intuitive predicate.
1867+--
1868+--     Some alternatives: 1) P_True b and P_False b (defined directly as
1869+--     desired) 1) bassertion b false (adds relevant argument to bassertion)
1870+--     2) ((bassertion (!b)) st) (clearer, but less direct).`
1871+
1872+theorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
1873+    ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1874+  simp [h]
1875+
1876+-- Here `simp` is able to find that `b.eval st` is assumed to be `false` (by
1877+-- rewriting with `h`), notice that the goal claims it is `true`, and use the
1878+-- resulting contradiction to complete the proof.
1879+
1880+-- Note to developers (One An  @meluge):
1881+--     The Rocq proof is the single tactic `congruence`. Using simp seems to
1882+--     work but should we build our own `congruence` tactic?
1883+
1884+-- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals and prove it
1885+-- correct.
1886+
1887+-- The statement of the rule reads: given `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1888+-- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1889+-- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1890+
1891+-- That is (unwrapping the notations):
1892+
1893+--   theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
1894+--       (htrue : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ bassertion b st) c1 Q)
1895+--       (hfalse : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ ¬ (bassertion b st)) c2 Q) :
1896+--       ValidHoareTriple P (Com.cond b c1 c2) Q
1897+
1898+theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
1899+    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1900+    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1901+  intro st st' hE hP
1902+  inversion hE with
1903+  | ifTrue hb hc => exact htrue _ _ hc ⟨hP, hb⟩
1904+  | ifFalse hb hc => exact hfalse _ _ hc ⟨hP, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
1905+
1906+-- #### Example
1907+
1908+-- Here is a formal proof that the program we used to motivate the rule
1909+-- satisfies the specification we wanted.
1910+
1911+theorem if_example :
1912+    {{True}}
1913+      if (X = 0) {
1914+        Y := 2;
1915+      } else {
1916+        Y := X + 1;
1917+      }
1918+    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1919+  apply hoare_if
1920+  · -- Then
1921+    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1922+    · apply hoare_asgn
1923+    · -- `assertion_auto` makes no progress here
1924+      unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1925+      intro st ⟨_, h⟩
1926+      simp only [Bexp.eval_eq, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num, beq_iff_eq] at h
1927+      rw [TotalMap.update_neq (by decide), TotalMap.update_eq, h]
1928+      simp
1929+  · -- Else
1930+    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1931+    · apply hoare_asgn
1932+    · assertion_auto
1933+
1934+-- As we did earlier, it would be nice to eliminate all the low-level proof
1935+-- script that isn't about the Hoare rules. Unfortunately, the
1936+-- `assertion_auto` tactic we wrote wasn't quite up to the job. Looking at the
1937+-- proof of `if_example`, we can see why: we had to unfold a definition
1938+-- (`bassertion`) that we didn't need in earlier proofs. (The step from the
1939+-- boolean equality test `st[X] == 0` to the equation `st[X] = 0` is handled
1940+-- by lemmas `simp` already knows, such as `beq_iff_eq`.) So, let's add the
1941+-- unfolding into our tactic.
1942+
1943+-- Note to developers:
1944+--     HIDE: MRC'20: There's probably a better way to engineer this. I don't
1945+--     know Ltac very well though.
1946+
1947+/-- Like `assertion_auto`, but also unfolds `bassertion`, so that facts
1948+about the boolean guards of conditionals and loops become available. -/
1949+macro "assertion_auto'" : tactic =>
1950+  `(tactic| (intros
1951+             <;> try (simp [assertImplies_def, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
1952+                            TotalMap.update, TotalMap.getElem_def,
1953+                            W, X, Y, Z] at *)
1954+             <;> try lia))
1955+
1956+-- Now the proof is quite streamlined.
1957+
1958+theorem if_example'' :
1959+    {{True}}
1960+      if (X = 0) {
1961+        Y := 2;
1962+      } else {
1963+        Y := X + 1;
1964+      }
1965+    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1966+  apply hoare_if
1967+  · apply hoare_consequence_pre
1968+    · apply hoare_asgn
1969+    · assertion_auto'
1970+  · apply hoare_consequence_pre
1971+    · apply hoare_asgn
1972+    · assertion_auto'
1973+
1974+-- We can even shorten it a little bit more.
1975+
1976+theorem if_example''' :
1977+    {{True}}
1978+      if (X = 0) {
1979+        Y := 2;
1980+      } else {
1981+        Y := X + 1;
1982+      }
1983+    {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1984+  apply hoare_if <;> apply hoare_consequence_pre <;>
1985+    (try apply hoare_asgn) <;> try assertion_auto'
1986+
1987+-- Note to developers (Claude):
1988+--     At this point the Rocq source defines a further refinement
1989+--     `assertion_auto''` that also rewrites with `leb_le`, "for
1990+--     inequalities". In Lean the boolean comparisons produced by `Bexp.eval`
1991+--     are already reduced by `simp`'s standard `decide`/`==` lemmas, so
1992+--     `assertion_auto'` handles inequalities as it stands and no
1993+--     `assertion_auto''` is needed (nor the later `assertion_auto'''`, whose
1994+--     extra `negb`/`not_false` rewrites `simp` also covers); occurrences of
1995+--     both in the Rocq text are rendered as `assertion_auto'`.
1996+
1997+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus ⭐⭐
1998+
1999+-- Prove the theorem below using `hoare_if`. Do not use
2000+-- `unfold
2001+-- ValidHoareTriple`. The `assertion_auto'` tactic we just defined may
2002+-- be useful.
2003+
2004+theorem if_minus_plus :
2005+    {{True}}
2006+      if (X ≤ Y) {
2007+        Z := Y - X;
2008+      } else {
2009+        Y := X + Z;
2010+      }
2011+    {{Y = X + Z}} := by
2012+  sorry
2013+
2014+-- #### Exercise: One-sided conditionals
2015+
2016+-- Note to developers:
2017+--     HIDE: Question from 2012, Midterm 2. One-sided conditionals.
2018+
2019+-- In this exercise we consider extending Imp with "one-sided conditionals" of
2020+-- the form `if1 (b) { c }`. Here `b` is a boolean expression, and `c` is a
2021+-- command. If `b` evaluates to `true`, then command `c` is evaluated. If `b`
2022+-- evaluates to `false`, then `if1 (b) { c }` does nothing.
2023+
2024+-- We recommend that you complete this exercise before attempting the ones
2025+-- that follow, as it should help solidify your understanding of the material.
2026+
2027+-- The first step is to extend the syntax of commands and introduce the usual
2028+-- notations. (We've done this for you, in a separate namespace to prevent
2029+-- polluting the global name space. The `scoped` notations below are active
2030+-- only inside `namespace If1`.)
2031+
2032+end -- closes `open scoped ValidHoareTriple`
2033+namespace If1
2034+
2035+inductive Com : Type where
2036+  | skip : Com
2037+  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2038+  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2039+  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2040+  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2041+  | if1 : Bexp → Com → Com
2042+
2043+/-- If1 commands: Imp commands plus `if1` -/
2044+declare_syntax_cat if1_com
2045+/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
2046+syntax ident ";" : if1_com
2047+/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
2048+syntax if1_com ppDedent(ppLine if1_com) : if1_com
2049+/-- Assignment -/
2050+syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : if1_com
2051+/-- Conditional -/
2052+syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2053+/-- Loop -/
2054+syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2055+/-- One-sided conditional -/
2056+syntax "if1 " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2057+/-- Escape to Lean -/
2058+syntax:max "~" term:max : if1_com
2059+
2060+/-- Include an If1 command in Lean code -/
2061+syntax:min "imp1" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2062+
2063+open Lean in
2064+macro_rules
2065+  | `(imp1 { $x:ident ; }) =>
2066+    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2067+    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2068+  | `(imp1 { $c1 $c2 }) =>
2069+    `(Com.seq (imp1 {$c1}) (imp1 {$c2}))
2070+  | `(imp1 { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
2071+    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2072+  | `(imp1 { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2073+    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp1 {$c1}) (imp1 {$c2}))
2074+  | `(imp1 { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2075+    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp1 {$c}))
2076+  | `(imp1 { if1 ($b) {$c} }) =>
2077+    `(Com.if1 (bexp {$b}) (imp1 {$c}))
2078+  | `(imp1 { ~$c }) =>
2079+    pure c
2080+
2081+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if1_ceval ⭐⭐
2082+
2083+-- Add two new evaluation rules to relation `Com.EvalR`, below, for `if1`. Let
2084+-- the rules for `if` guide you.
2085+
2086+inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
2087+  | skip (st : State) :
2088+      EvalR (imp1 {skip;}) st st
2089+  | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
2090+      EvalR (imp1 {x := ~a;}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
2091+  | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' st'' : State)
2092+      (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
2093+      EvalR (imp1 {~c1 ~c2}) st st''
2094+  | ifTrue (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
2095+      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
2096+      EvalR (imp1 {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2097+  | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
2098+      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
2099+      EvalR (imp1 {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2100+  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2101+      EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st st
2102+  | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2103+      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2104+      (hloop : EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :
2105+      EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st st''
2106+-- FILL IN HERE
2107+
2108+scoped notation:40 (priority := high) st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 =>
2109+  Com.EvalR c st0 st1
2110+scoped syntax:40 (priority := high) term:41 " =[ " if1_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
2111+scoped macro_rules
2112+  | `($st0 =[ $c:if1_com ]=> $st1) => `($st0 =[ imp1 { $c } ]=> $st1)

2126+-- Now we have to repeat the definition and notation of Hoare triples, so that
2127+-- they will use the updated `Com` type.
2128+
2129+def ValidHoareTriple
2130+    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2131+  ∀ st st',
2132+    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
2133+    P st →
2134+    Q st'

2141+macro_rules
2142+  | `({{ $P }} $c:if1_com {{ $Q }}) =>
2143+      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp1 { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
2144+
2145+end ValidHoareTriple

2175+-- Before the next exercise, we need to restate the Hoare rules of consequence
2176+-- (for preconditions) and assignment for the new `Com` type.
2177+
2178+theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
2179+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
2180+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
2181+  intro st st' heval hpre
2182+  exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
2183+
2184+theorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
2185+    {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by
2186+  intro st st' heval hQ
2187+  inversion heval with
2188+  | asgn n h =>
2189+    subst h
2190+    exact hQ
