2220+
2221+-- ### While Loops
2222+
2223+-- The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a *command
2224+-- invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion whose truth is guaranteed
2225+-- after executing a command, assuming it is true before.
2226+
2227+-- That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
2228+
2229+--   {{P}} c {{P}}
2230+
2231+-- holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily become false in
2232+-- the middle of executing `c`, but by the end of `c` it must be restored.
2233+
2234+-- As a first attempt at a `while` rule, we could try:
2235+
2236+--          {{P}} c {{P}}
2237+--   ---------------------------
2238+--   {{P} while b do c end {{P}}
2239+
2240+-- This rule is valid: if `P` is a command invariant of `c`, as the premise
2241+-- requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body executes, `P` is
2242+-- going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
2243+
2244+-- But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the loop
2245+-- terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the postcondition
2246+-- in the conclusion:
2247+
2248+--           {{P}} c {{P}}
2249+--   ---------------------------------
2250+--   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2251+
2252+-- Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can also
2253+-- strengthen the precondition in the premise:
2254+
2255+--         {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2256+--   --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
2257+--   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2258+
2259+-- That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip` and
2260+-- conditionals:
2261+
2262+-- - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that the
2263+--   precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
2264+
2265+-- - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
2266+--   subcommand.
2267+
2268+-- Note to developers:
2269+--     HIDE: The big comment will not display nicely. But I guess it's
2270+--     folded...
2271+
2272+theorem hoare_while (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2273+    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
2274+    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
2275+  intro st st' heval hP
2276+  /- We proceed by induction on `heval`, because, in the "keep
2277+  looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
2278+  of just `c`. The auxiliary statement `key` generalizes over an
2279+  arbitrary command, together with an equation remembering that the
2280+  command is the original loop; otherwise, that information would
2281+  be lost in the induction. The cases for commands other than
2282+  `while` are dismissed because their equations are contradictory. -/
2283+  have key : ∀ (cmd : Com) (s s' : State), (s =[ cmd ]=> s') →
2284+      cmd = (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) → P s →
2285+      P s' ∧ ¬ bassertion b s' := by
2286+    intro cmd s s' hev
2287+    induction hev with
2288+    | whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
2289+        intro heq hp
2290+        injection heq with e1 _
2291+        subst e1
2292+        exact ⟨hp, bexp_eval_false _ _ hb⟩
2293+    | whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
2294+        intro heq hp
2295+        injection heq with e1 e2
2296+        subst e1 e2
2297+        exact ih2 rfl (hhoare _ _ hc ⟨hp, hb⟩)
2298+    | skip s0 => intro heq; simp at heq
2299+    | asgn s0 a n x h => intro heq; simp at heq
2300+    | seq c1 c2 s0 s0' s0'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp at heq
2301+    | ifTrue s0 s0' b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
2302+    | ifFalse s0 s0' b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
2303+  exact key _ st st' heval rfl hP
2304+
2305+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce  @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
2306+--     This definition / discussion could be clearer.
2307+
2308+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce  @bcpierce00, before next release, 2023):
2309+--     `Maja says: The wording of "we will never enter the
2310+--     loop" could definitely be improved. As is, it suggests a situation
2311+--     where the loop condition itself can never be satisfied. I suspect that
2312+--     a previous draft included a discussion that explicitly placed {{ P }}
2313+--     before the while, perhaps along the lines of "a loop invariant P of
2314+--     [while b do c end] is also an invariant of [while b do c end]" (which
2315+--     is, FWIW, a (somewhat obtuse) way of stating a weaker variant of
2316+--     hoare_while, without the ~b in the postcondition). Combined with the
2317+--     fact that it is supposed to justify a somewhat surprising and
2318+--     unexpected fact — [X = 0] is not what I would intuitively consider an
2319+--     invariant of this loop — this sentence ends up being quite confusing.
2320+--     I only understood it when I came back to find this excerpt.`
2321+
2322+-- We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
2323+
2324+--   {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2325+
2326+-- is a valid Hoare triple.
2327+
2328+-- This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body whenever the
2329+-- loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`, this holds trivially since the
2330+-- precondition is false.
2331+
2332+-- For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
2333+
2334+--   while X = 2 do X := 1 end
2335+
2336+-- since the program will never enter the loop.
2337+
2338+-- _Quiz:_
2339+
2340+-- Is the assertion
2341+
2342+--   Y = 0
2343+
2344+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2345+
2346+--   while X < 100 do X := X + 1 end
2347+
2348+-- (A) Yes
2349+
2350+-- (B) No
2351+
2352+-- _Quiz:_
2353+
2354+-- Is the assertion
2355+
2356+--   X = 0
2357+
2358+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2359+
2360+--   while X < 100 do X := X + 1 end
2361+
2362+-- (A) Yes
2363+
2364+-- (B) No
2365+
2366+-- _Quiz:_
2367+
2368+-- Is the assertion
2369+
2370+--   X < Y
2371+
2372+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2373+
2374+--   while true do X := X + 1; Y := Y + 1 end
2375+
2376+-- (A) Yes
2377+
2378+-- (B) No
2379+
2380+-- _Quiz:_
2381+
2382+-- Is the assertion
2383+
2384+--   X = Y + Z
2385+
2386+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2387+
2388+--   while Y > 10 do Y := Y - 1; Z := Z + 1 end
2389+
2390+-- (A) Yes
2391+
2392+-- (B) No
2393+
2394+-- Note to developers (before next release):
2395+--     This last quiz should be turned into a discussion in the text, at least
2396+--     in the full version -- indeed, maybe all these should be turned into a
2397+--     long discussion of what it means to be a loop invariant -- I think that
2398+--     would be pretty helpful.
2399+
2400+-- The program
2401+
2402+--   while Y > 10 do Y := Y - 1; Z := Z + 1 end
2403+
2404+-- admits an interesting loop invariant:
2405+
2406+--   X = Y + Z
2407+
2408+-- Note that this doesn't contradict the loop guard but neither is it a
2409+-- command invariant of
2410+
2411+--   Y := Y - 1; Z := Z + 1
2412+
2413+-- since, if X = 5, Y = 0 and Z = 5, running the command will set Y + Z to 6.
2414+-- The loop guard `Y > 10` guarantees that this will not be the case. We will
2415+-- see many such loop invariants in the following chapter.
2416+
2417+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce  @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
2418+--     What is this example doing here?? Needs some text.
2419+
2420+theorem while_example :
2421+    {{X ≤ 3}}
2422+      while (X ≤ 2) {
2423+        X := X + 1;
2424+      }
2425+    {{X = 3}} := by
2426+  apply hoare_consequence_post
2427+  · apply hoare_while
2428+    apply hoare_consequence_pre
2429+    · apply hoare_asgn
2430+    · assertion_auto'
2431+  · assertion_auto'
2432+

2434+--     `HIDE: CJC: Maybe also a good place to talk about the structure of
2435+--     our logic - that we've set up the hoare_* lemmas and they are all
2436+--     the reasoning about Hoare triples that they should have to use (in
2437+--     both formal or informal proofs)?  Probably should talk about this
2438+--     somewhere or else we'll get back lots of proofs that unfold
2439+--     ValidHoareTriple and reason at a low level everywhere.
2440+--
2441+--     BCP 21: I think we do this now?`
2442+
2443+-- _Quiz:_
2444+
2445+-- Is the assertion
2446+
2447+--   X > 0
2448+
2449+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2450+
2451+--   while X = 0 do X := X - 1 end
2452+
2453+-- (A) Yes
2454+
2455+-- (B) No
2456+
2457+-- _Quiz:_
2458+
2459+-- Is the assertion
2460+
2461+--   X < 100
2462+
2463+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2464+
2465+--   while X < 100 do X := X + 1 end
2466+
2467+-- (A) Yes
2468+
2469+-- (B) No
2470+
2471+-- _Quiz:_
2472+
2473+-- Is the assertion
2474+
2475+--   X > 10
2476+
2477+-- a loop invariant of the following?
2478+
2479+--   while X > 10 do X := X + 1 end
2480+
2481+-- (A) Yes
2482+
2483+-- (B) No
2484+
2485+-- If the loop never terminates, any postcondition will work.
2486+
2487+theorem always_loop_hoare (Q : Assertion) :
2488+    {{True}} while (true) { skip; } {{ Q }} := by
2489+  apply hoare_consequence_post
2490+  · apply hoare_while
2491+    apply hoare_post_true
2492+    intro st
2493+    exact True.intro
2494+  · intro st ⟨_hinv, hguard⟩
2495+    exact absurd rfl hguard
2496+
2497+-- Of course, this result is not surprising if we remember that the definition
2498+-- of `ValidHoareTriple` asserts that the postcondition must hold *only* when
2499+-- the command terminates. If the command doesn't terminate, we can prove
2500+-- anything we like about the post-condition.
2501+
2502+-- Hoare rules that specify what happens *if* commands terminate, without
2503+-- proving that they do, are said to describe a logic of *partial*
2504+-- correctness. It is also possible to give Hoare rules for *total*
2505+-- correctness, which additionally specifies that commands must terminate.
2506+-- Total correctness is out of the scope of this textbook.
2507+
2508+-- #### Exercise: `repeat`
2509+
2510+-- Note to developers:
2511+--     HIDE: I (BCP) think I see a much simpler way to do the 'for' stuff.
2512+--     Instead of `for x from a to b do c` define `for x downfrom a do c` that
2513+--     steps from a down to 0. This will be much simpler to specify, though
2514+--     still an interesting challenge. (CJC: This still seemed hard to me, but
2515+--     I'm deleting it for now to get things looking right)
2516+--
2517+--     HIDE: Coming up with the precise rule for REPEAT is tricky, and so is
2518+--     proving formally that the precise rule passes the litmus test (at this
2519+--     point we only ask them to convince themselves informally there).
2520+
2521+-- In this exercise, we'll add a new command to our language of commands:
2522+-- `repeat { c } until (b)`. You will write the evaluation rule for `repeat`
2523+-- and add a new Hoare rule to the language for programs involving it.
2524+
2525+end
2526+namespace RepeatExercise
2527+
2528+inductive Com : Type where
2529+  | skip : Com
2530+  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2531+  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2532+  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2533+  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2534+  | repeatUntil : Com → Bexp → Com
2535+
2536+-- `repeat` behaves like `while`, except that the loop guard is checked
2537+-- *after* each execution of the body, with the loop repeating as long as the
2538+-- guard stays *false*. Because of this, the body will always execute at least
2539+-- once.
2540+
2541+/-- Repeat-Imp commands: Imp commands plus `repeat` -/
2542+declare_syntax_cat rpt_com
2543+/-- Repeat loop -/
2544+syntax "repeat" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") " until " "(" imp_bexp ")" : rpt_com
2545+
2546+/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
2547+syntax ident ";" : rpt_com
2548+/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
2549+syntax rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine rpt_com) : rpt_com
2550+/-- Assignment -/
2551+syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : rpt_com
2552+/-- Conditional -/
2553+syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : rpt_com
2554+/-- Loop -/
2555+syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : rpt_com
2556+/-- Escape to Lean -/
2557+syntax:max "~" term:max : rpt_com
2558+
2559+/-- Include a Repeat-Imp command in Lean code -/
2560+syntax:min "impr" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine rpt_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2561+
2562+open Lean in
2563+macro_rules
2564+  | `(impr { $x:ident ; }) =>
2565+    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2566+    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2567+  | `(impr { $c1 $c2 }) =>
2568+    `(Com.seq (impr {$c1}) (impr {$c2}))
2569+  | `(impr { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
2570+    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2571+  | `(impr { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2572+    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (impr {$c1}) (impr {$c2}))
2573+  | `(impr { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2574+    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (impr {$c}))
2575+  | `(impr { repeat {$c} until ($b) }) =>
2576+    `(Com.repeatUntil (impr {$c}) (bexp {$b}))
2577+  | `(impr { ~$c }) =>
2578+    pure c
2579+
2580+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): hoare_repeat (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
2581+
2582+-- Add new rules for `repeat` to `Com.EvalR` below. You can use the rules for
2583+-- `while` as a guide, but remember that the body of a `repeat` should always
2584+-- execute at least once, and that the loop ends when the guard becomes true.
2585+
2586+inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
2587+  | skip (st : State) :
2588+      EvalR (impr {skip;}) st st
2589+  | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
2590+      EvalR (impr {x := ~a;}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
2591+  | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' st'' : State)
2592+      (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
2593+      EvalR (impr {~c1 ~c2}) st st''
2594+  | ifTrue (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
2595+      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
2596+      EvalR (impr {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2597+  | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
2598+      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
2599+      EvalR (impr {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2600+  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2601+      EvalR (impr {while (~b) {~c} }) st st
2602+  | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2603+      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2604+      (hloop : EvalR (impr {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :
2605+      EvalR (impr {while (~b) {~c} }) st st''
2606+-- FILL IN HERE
2607+
2608+scoped notation:40 (priority := high) st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 =>
2609+  Com.EvalR c st0 st1
2610+scoped syntax:40 (priority := high) term:41 " =[ " rpt_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
2611+scoped macro_rules
2612+  | `($st0 =[ $c:rpt_com ]=> $st1) => `($st0 =[ impr { $c } ]=> $st1)
2613+
2614+-- A couple of definitions from above, copied here so they use the new
2615+-- `Com.EvalR`.
2616+
2617+def ValidHoareTriple (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2618+  ∀ st st', (st =[ c ]=> st') → P st → Q st'
2619+
2620+namespace ValidHoareTriple
2621+
2622+/-- Hoare triple over Repeat-Imp commands -/
2623+scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " rpt_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
2624+
2625+macro_rules
2626+  | `({{ $P }} $c:rpt_com {{ $Q }}) =>
2627+      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (impr { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
2628+
2629+end ValidHoareTriple
2630+
2631+open scoped ValidHoareTriple

2633+-- To make sure you've got the evaluation rules for `repeat` right, prove that
2634+-- `ex1_repeat` evaluates correctly.
2635+
2636+def ex1_repeat : Com :=
2637+  impr {
2638+    repeat {
2639+      X := 1;
2640+      Y := Y + 1;
2641+    } until (X = 1)
2642+  }
2643+
2644+theorem ex1_repeat_works :
2645+    ∅ =[ ex1_repeat ]=> (Y →ₜ 1 ; X →ₜ 1 ; ∅) := by
2646+  sorry

2648+-- Now state and prove a theorem, `hoare_repeat`, that expresses an
2649+-- appropriate proof rule for `repeat` commands. Use `hoare_while` as a model,
2650+-- and try to make your rule as precise as possible.
2651+
2652+-- FILL IN HERE
2653+
2654+-- For full credit, make sure (informally) that your rule can be used to prove
2655+-- the following valid Hoare triple:
2656+
2657+--   {{ X > 0 }}
2658+--   repeat {
2659+--     Y := X;
2660+--     X := X - 1;
2661+--   } until (X = 0)
2662+--   {{ X = 0 ∧ Y > 0 }}

2675+
2676+-- ## Summary
2677+
2678+-- So far, we've introduced Hoare Logic as a tool for reasoning about Imp
2679+-- programs.
2680+
2681+-- The rules of Hoare Logic are:
2682+
2683+--          --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
2684+--          {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
2685+
2686+--          --------------------  (hoare_skip)
2687+--          {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
2688+
2689+--            {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
2690+--            {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
2691+--           ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
2692+--           {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
2693+
2694+--           {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
2695+--           {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
2696+--   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
2697+--   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
2698+
2699+--            {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2700+--     -----------------------------------  (hoare_while)
2701+--     {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
2702+
2703+--             {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
2704+--                P ->> P'
2705+--                Q' ->> Q
2706+--      -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
2707+--             {{P}} c {{Q}}
2708+
2709+-- Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules of Hoare
2710+-- logic, and prove that the definitions are sound. Having done so, we can go
2711+-- on and work *within* Hoare logic to prove that particular programs satisfy
2712+-- particular Hoare triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how Hoare logic is
2713+-- can be used to prove that more interesting programs satisfy interesting
2714+-- specifications of their behavior.
2715+
2716+-- Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing the definition of
2717+-- Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules of Hoare logic as a closed
2718+-- world for reasoning about programs.
2719+
2720+-- ## Additional Exercises
2721+
2722+-- ### Havoc
2723+
2724+-- In this exercise, we will derive proof rules for a `havoc` command, which
2725+-- is similar to the nondeterministic `any` expression from the the Imp
2726+-- chapter.
2727+
2728+-- First, we enclose this work in a separate namespace, and recall the syntax
2729+-- and big-step semantics of Himp commands.
2730+
2731+namespace Himp
2732+
2733+inductive Com : Type where
2734+  | skip : Com
2735+  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2736+  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2737+  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2738+  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2739+  | havoc : Ident → Com
2740+
2741+/-- Himp commands: Imp commands plus `havoc` -/
2742+declare_syntax_cat himp_com
2743+/-- Havoc: set a variable to a nondeterministically chosen number
2744+(`havoc x;`).  As with `skip`, the word `havoc` is not reserved: the
2745+production accepts any identifier and the macro below rejects
2746+everything except `havoc`. -/
2747+syntax ident ident ";" : himp_com
2748+
2749+/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
2750+syntax ident ";" : himp_com
2751+/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
2752+syntax himp_com ppDedent(ppLine himp_com) : himp_com
2753+/-- Assignment -/
2754+syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : himp_com
2755+/-- Conditional -/
2756+syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine himp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine himp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : himp_com
2757+/-- Loop -/
2758+syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine himp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : himp_com
2759+/-- Escape to Lean -/
2760+syntax:max "~" term:max : himp_com
2761+
2762+/-- Include a Himp command in Lean code -/
2763+syntax:min "imph" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine himp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2764+
2765+open Lean in
2766+macro_rules
2767+  | `(imph { $x:ident ; }) =>
2768+    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2769+    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2770+  | `(imph { $c1 $c2 }) =>
2771+    `(Com.seq (imph {$c1}) (imph {$c2}))
2772+  | `(imph { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
2773+    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2774+  | `(imph { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2775+    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imph {$c1}) (imph {$c2}))
2776+  | `(imph { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2777+    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imph {$c}))
2778+  | `(imph { $h:ident $x:ident ; }) =>
2779+    if h.getId == `havoc then `(Com.havoc $x)
2780+    else Macro.throwErrorAt h s!"expected 'havoc', got '{h.getId}'"
2781+  | `(imph { ~$c }) =>
2782+    pure c
2783+
2784+inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
2785+  | skip (st : State) :
2786+      EvalR (imph {skip;}) st st
2787+  | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
2788+      EvalR (imph {x := ~a;}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
2789+  | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' st'' : State)
2790+      (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
2791+      EvalR (imph {~c1 ~c2}) st st''
2792+  | ifTrue (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
2793+      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
2794+      EvalR (imph {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2795+  | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
2796+      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
2797+      EvalR (imph {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2798+  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2799+      EvalR (imph {while (~b) {~c} }) st st
2800+  | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2801+      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2802+      (hloop : EvalR (imph {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :
2803+      EvalR (imph {while (~b) {~c} }) st st''
2804+  | havoc (st : State) (x : Ident) (n : Nat) :
2805+      EvalR (imph {havoc x;}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
2806+
2807+scoped notation:40 (priority := high) st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 =>
2808+  Com.EvalR c st0 st1
2809+scoped syntax:40 (priority := high) term:41 " =[ " himp_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
2810+scoped macro_rules
2811+  | `($st0 =[ $c:himp_com ]=> $st1) => `($st0 =[ imph { $c } ]=> $st1)
2812+
2813+-- The definition of Hoare triples is exactly as before.
2814+
2815+def ValidHoareTriple (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2816+  ∀ st st', (st =[ c ]=> st') → P st → Q st'
2817+
2818+namespace ValidHoareTriple
2819+
2820+/-- Hoare triple over Himp commands -/
2821+scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " himp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
2822+
2823+macro_rules
2824+  | `({{ $P }} $c:himp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
2825+      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imph { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
2826+
2827+end ValidHoareTriple
2828+
2829+open scoped ValidHoareTriple
2830+
2831+-- And the precondition consequence rule is exactly as before.
2832+
2833+theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
2834+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
2835+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
2836+  intro st st' heval hpre
2837+  exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
2838+
2839+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): hoare_havoc (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
2840+
2841+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce  @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
2842+--     This exercise turns out to be quite hard -- a lot of people get stuck.
2843+--     We should make it advanced the next time through. BCP 23: Made it
2844+--     advanced. Can we also explain it better?
2845+
2846+-- Complete the Hoare rule for `havoc` commands below by defining `havoc_pre`,
2847+-- and prove that the resulting rule is correct.
2848+
2849+def havoc_pre (x : Ident) (Q : Assertion) (st : State) : Prop :=
2850+  sorry
2851+
2852+theorem hoare_havoc (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) :
2853+    {{ fun st => havoc_pre x Q st }} havoc x; {{ Q }} := by
2854+  sorry
2855+
2856+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): havoc_post (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
2857+
2858+-- Complete the following proof without changing any of the provided commands.
2859+-- If you find that it can't be completed, your definition of `havoc_pre` is
2860+-- probably too strong. Find a way to relax it so that `havoc_post` can be
2861+-- proved.
2862+
2863+-- Hint: the `assertion_auto` tactics we've built won't help you here. You
2864+-- need to proceed manually.
2865+
2866+-- Note to developers (before next release):
2867+--     This exercise is kind of weird. Should probably be optional.
2868+
2869+theorem havoc_post (P : Assertion) (x : Ident) :
2870+    {{ P }} havoc x;
2871+    {{ fun st => ∃ (n : Nat), ({{ P [x ↦ ~(Aexp.num n)] }}) st }} := by
2872+  apply hoare_consequence_pre
2873+  · apply hoare_havoc
2874+  ·
2875+    sorry
2876+
2877+end Himp
2878+
2879+-- ### Assert and Assume
2880+
2881+-- Note to developers (Claude):
2882+--     The Rocq exercise region extends to End HoareAssertAssume. The
2883+--     directive here covers only the initial student tasks because Verso
2884+--     cannot compile the whole module as one block.
2885+
2886+-- In this exercise, we will extend IMP with two commands, `assert` and
2887+-- `assume`. Both commands are ways to indicate that a certain assertion
2888+-- should hold any time this part of the program is reached. However they
2889+-- differ as follows:
2890+
2891+-- - If an `assert` statement fails, it causes the program to go into an error
2892+--   state and exit.
2893+
2894+-- - If an `assume` statement fails, the program fails to evaluate at all. In
2895+--   other words, the program gets stuck and has no final state.
2896+
2897+-- The new set of commands is:
2898+
2899+namespace HoareAssertAssume
2900+
2901+inductive Com : Type where
2902+  | skip : Com
2903+  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2904+  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2905+  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2906+  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2907+  | assert : Bexp → Com
2908+  | assume : Bexp → Com
2909+
2910+-- Note to developers:
2911+--     NOTATION: LATER: Reconsider these precedences
2912+
2913+/-- Imp commands plus `assert` and `assume` -/
2914+declare_syntax_cat haa_com
2915+/-- Assert / assume (`assert (b);`, `assume (b);`).  As with `skip`, the
2916+words `assert` and `assume` are not reserved: the production accepts any
2917+identifier and the macro below rejects everything else. -/
2918+syntax ident " (" imp_bexp ")" ";" : haa_com
2919+
2920+/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
2921+syntax ident ";" : haa_com
2922+/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
2923+syntax haa_com ppDedent(ppLine haa_com) : haa_com
2924+/-- Assignment -/
2925+syntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : haa_com
2926+/-- Conditional -/
2927+syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : haa_com
2928+/-- Loop -/
2929+syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : haa_com
2930+/-- Escape to Lean -/
2931+syntax:max "~" term:max : haa_com
2932+
2933+/-- Include an assert/assume-Imp command in Lean code -/
2934+syntax:min "impa" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine haa_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2935+
2936+open Lean in
2937+macro_rules
2938+  | `(impa { $x:ident ; }) =>
2939+    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2940+    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2941+  | `(impa { $h:ident ($b) ; }) =>
2942+    if h.getId == `assert then `(Com.assert (bexp {$b}))
2943+    else if h.getId == `assume then `(Com.assume (bexp {$b}))
2944+    else Macro.throwErrorAt h s!"expected 'assert' or 'assume', got '{h.getId}'"
2945+  | `(impa { $c1 $c2 }) =>
2946+    `(Com.seq (impa {$c1}) (impa {$c2}))
2947+  | `(impa { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
2948+    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2949+  | `(impa { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2950+    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (impa {$c1}) (impa {$c2}))
2951+  | `(impa { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2952+    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (impa {$c}))
2953+  | `(impa { ~$c }) =>
2954+    pure c
2955+
2956+-- To define the behavior of `assert` and `assume`, we need to add notation
2957+-- for an error, which indicates that an assertion has failed. We modify the
2958+-- `Com.EvalR` relation, therefore, so that it relates a start state to either
2959+-- an end state or to `error`. The `Result` type indicates the end value of a
2960+-- program, either a state or an error:
2961+
2962+inductive Result : Type where
2963+  | normal : State → Result
2964+  | error : Result
2965+
2966+-- Now we are ready to give you the evaluation relation for the new language.
2967+
2968+inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → Result → Prop where
2969+  /- Old rules, several modified -/
2970+  | skip (st : State) :
2971+      EvalR (impa {skip;}) st (.normal st)
2972+  | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
2973+      EvalR (impa {x := ~a;}) st (.normal (x →ₜ n ; st))
2974+  | seqNormal (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' : State) (r : Result)
2975+      (h1 : EvalR c1 st (.normal st')) (h2 : EvalR c2 st' r) :
2976+      EvalR (impa {~c1 ~c2}) st r
2977+  | seqError (c1 c2 : Com) (st : State) (h : EvalR c1 st .error) :
2978+      EvalR (impa {~c1 ~c2}) st .error
2979+  | ifTrue (st : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
2980+      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c1 st r) :
2981+      EvalR (impa {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
2982+  | ifFalse (st : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
2983+      (hb : b.eval st = false) (hc : EvalR c2 st r) :
2984+      EvalR (impa {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
2985+  | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2986+      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st (.normal st)
2987+  | whileTrueNormal (st st' : State) (r : Result) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2988+      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st (.normal st'))
2989+      (hloop : EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st' r) :
2990+      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st r
2991+  | whileTrueError (st : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2992+      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st .error) :
2993+      EvalR (impa {while (~b) {~c} }) st .error
2994+  /- Rules for Assert and Assume -/
2995+  | assertTrue (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = true) :
2996+      EvalR (impa {assert (~b);}) st (.normal st)
2997+  | assertFalse (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2998+      EvalR (impa {assert (~b);}) st .error
2999+  | assume (st : State) (b : Bexp) (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3000+      EvalR (impa {assume (~b);}) st (.normal st)
3001+
3002+scoped notation:40 (priority := high) st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " r:41 =>
3003+  Com.EvalR c st0 r
3004+scoped syntax:40 (priority := high) term:41 " =[ " haa_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
3005+scoped macro_rules
3006+  | `($st0 =[ $c:haa_com ]=> $r) => `($st0 =[ impa { $c } ]=> $r)
3007+
3008+-- We redefine hoare triples: Now, `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` means that, whenever
3009+-- `c` is started in a state satisfying `P`, and terminates with result `r`,
3010+-- then `r` is not an error and the state of `r` satisfies `Q`.
3011+
3012+def ValidHoareTriple
3013+    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
3014+  ∀ st r,
3015+    (st =[ c ]=> r) → P st →
3016+    (∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q st')
3017+
3018+namespace ValidHoareTriple
3019+
3020+/-- Hoare triple over assert/assume-Imp commands -/
3021+scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " haa_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
3022+
3023+macro_rules
3024+  | `({{ $P }} $c:haa_com {{ $Q }}) =>
3025+      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (impa { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
3026+
3027+end ValidHoareTriple
3028+
3029+open scoped ValidHoareTriple
3030+
3031+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): assert_vs_assume ⭐⭐⭐⭐
3032+
3033+-- To test your understanding of this modification, give an example
3034+-- precondition and postcondition that are satisfied by the `assume` statement
3035+-- but not by the `assert` statement.
3036+
3037+theorem assert_assume_differ : ∃ (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion),
3038+    ({{ P }} assume (~b); {{ Q }})
3039+    ∧ ¬ ({{ P }} assert (~b); {{ Q }}) := by
3040+  sorry
3041+
3042+-- Then prove that any triple for an `assert` also works when `assert` is
3043+-- replaced by `assume`.
3044+
3045+theorem assert_implies_assume (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion)
3046+    (hhoare : {{ P }} assert (~b); {{ Q }}) :
3047+    {{ P }} assume (~b); {{ Q }} := by
3048+  sorry
3049+
3050+-- Next, here are proofs for the old hoare rules adapted to the new semantics.
3051+-- You don't need to do anything with these.
3052+
3053+theorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
3054+    {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by
3055+  unfold ValidHoareTriple
3056+  intro st r hE hQ
3057+  inversion hE with
3058+  | asgn n h =>
3059+    exists (x →ₜ n ; st)
3060+    subst h
3061+    exact ⟨rfl, hQ⟩
3062+
3063+theorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
3064+    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
3065+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
3066+  intro st r hc hP
3067+  apply hhoare st r
3068+  · assumption
3069+  · apply himp
3070+    assumption
3071+
3072+theorem hoare_consequence_post (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
3073+    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
3074+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
3075+  intro st r hc hP
3076+  unfold ValidHoareTriple at hhoare
3077+  have h : ∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q' st' := by
3078+    apply hhoare st <;> assumption
3079+  obtain ⟨st', hr, hQ'⟩ := h
3080+  exists st'
3081+  constructor
3082+  · assumption
3083+  · apply himp
3084+    assumption
3085+
3086+theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
3087+    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{R}}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
3088+    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{R}} := by
3089+  intro st r h12 pre
3090+  inversion h12 with
3091+  | seqNormal st' hc1 hc2 =>
3092+    apply h1
3093+    · apply hc2
3094+    · apply h2 at hc1
3095+      apply hc1 at pre
3096+      obtain ⟨st'', heq, hQ⟩ := pre
3097+      injection heq with e
3098+      subst e
3099+      assumption
3100+  | seqError hc1 =>
3101+    -- Find contradictory assumption
3102+    apply h2 at hc1
3103+    apply hc1 at pre
3104+    obtain ⟨st', hC, _⟩ := pre
3105+    simp at hC
3106+
3107+-- Here are the other proof rules (sanity check)
3108+
3109+theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
3110+    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
3111+  intro st r h hP
3112+  inversion h
3113+  exact ⟨st, rfl, hP⟩
3114+
3115+theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
3116+    (hTrue : {{ P ∧ b}} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hFalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b}} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
3117+    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
3118+  intro st r hE hP
3119+  inversion hE with
3120+  | ifTrue hb hc =>
3121+    -- b is true
3122+    apply hTrue st r
3123+    · assumption
3124+    · exact ⟨hP, hb⟩
3125+  | ifFalse hb hc =>
3126+    -- b is false
3127+    apply hFalse st r
3128+    · assumption
3129+    · exact ⟨hP, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
3130+
3131+theorem hoare_while (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
3132+    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
3133+    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{ P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
3134+  intro st r he hP
3135+  have key : ∀ (cmd : Com) (s : State) (r' : Result), (s =[ cmd ]=> r') →
3136+      cmd = (impa { while (~b) { ~c } }) → P s →
3137+      ∃ s', r' = Result.normal s' ∧ P s' ∧ ¬ bassertion b s' := by
3138+    intro cmd s r' hev
3139+    induction hev with
3140+    | whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
3141+        intro heq hp
3142+        injection heq with e1 _
3143+        subst e1
3144+        exact ⟨s0, rfl, hp, bexp_eval_false _ _ hb⟩
3145+    | whileTrueNormal s0 s0' r0 b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
3146+        intro heq hp
3147+        injection heq with e1 e2
3148+        subst e1 e2
3149+        apply ih2 rfl
3150+        obtain ⟨s1, heq1, hp1⟩ := hhoare _ _ hc ⟨hp, hb⟩
3151+        injection heq1 with e
3152+        subst e
3153+        exact hp1
3154+    | whileTrueError s0 b0 c0 hb hc =>
3155+        intro heq hp
3156+        injection heq with e1 e2
3157+        subst e1 e2
3158+        obtain ⟨s1, heq1, _⟩ := hhoare _ _ hc ⟨hp, hb⟩
3159+        simp at heq1
3160+    | skip s0 => intro heq; simp at heq
3161+    | asgn s0 a n x ha => intro heq; simp at heq
3162+    | seqNormal c1 c2 s0 s0' r0 hh1 hh2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp at heq
3163+    | seqError c1 c2 s0 hh ih => intro heq; simp at heq
3164+    | ifTrue s0 r0 b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
3165+    | ifFalse s0 r0 b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
3166+    | assertTrue s0 b0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
3167+    | assertFalse s0 b0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
3168+    | assume s0 b0 hb => intro heq; simp at heq
3169+  exact key _ st r he rfl hP
3170+
3171+-- Finally, state Hoare rules for `assert` and `assume` and use them to prove
3172+-- a simple program correct. Name your rules `hoare_assert` and
3173+-- `hoare_assume`.
3174+
3175+-- FILL IN HERE
3176+
3177+-- Use your rules to prove the following triple.
3178+
3179+theorem assert_assume_example :
3180+    {{True}}
3181+      assume (X = 1);
3182+      X := X + 1;
3183+      assert (X = 2);
3184+    {{True}} := by
3185+  sorry
3186+
3187+end HoareAssertAssume

21+/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/

25+/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,

30+/--
31+  `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,
32+  then solves away contradictory generated goals.
33+  `t` itself will also be generalized with a heterogeneous equality `heq`
34+  if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.
35+  * If `inversion +clear t` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
36+    along with `t` if there are no dependencies on it.
37+  * The form `inversion t with | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...` is supported,
38+    similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.
39+-/
40+syntax (name := inversion)
41+  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (colGe invAlts)+)? : tactic
42+
43+end Lean.Parser

45+namespace Lean.Meta

47+/--
48+  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
49+  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
50+  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
51+  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
52+  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
53+
54+  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
55+  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
56+  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
57+  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
58+
59+  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
60+-/
61+def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
62+    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
63+    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
64+  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
65+  unless ms.size == 1 do
66+    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
67+    else throwError m!"Failed"
68+  let mut mvs := ms
69+  let mut bis := bs
70+  let mut out : Expr := tp
71+  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
72+    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
73+    unless ms.size == 1 do
74+      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
75+    mvs := mvs ++ ms
76+    bis := bis ++ bs
77+    out := tp
78+  return (mvs, bis, out)
79+
80+/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
81+def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
82+  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
83+  return decl.userName
84+
85+/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
86+  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
87+  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
88+  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
89+  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
90+  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
91+
92+  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
93+partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
94+  match eqs with
95+  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
96+  | eq :: eqs =>
97+    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
98+      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
99+    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
100+    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
101+    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
102+
103+/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
104+def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
105+  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
106+    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
107+    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
108+    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
109+    else return some { s with
110+      mvarId := mvarId,
111+      subst  := subst,
112+      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
113+    }
114+
115+/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
116+  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
117+
118+  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
119+def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
120+  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
121+    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
122+    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
123+    return { s with mvarId }
124+
125+end Lean.Meta
126+
127+namespace Lean.Elab.Tactic
128+open Meta Term
129+
130+-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
131+-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
132+/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
133+macro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
134+
135+/--
136+  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
137+  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
138+  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
139+  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
140+  original `i`.
141+
142+  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
143+-/
144+elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
145+  let f ← elabTermForApply t
146+  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
147+    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
148+  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
149+  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
150+    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
151+      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
152+      catch _ => continue
153+  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
154+    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
155+  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
156+  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
157+
158+structure InversionConfig where
159+  clear : Bool := false
160+
161+declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
162+
163+open Cases in
164+def inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List CasesSubgoal) := withMainContext do
165+  let goal ← getMainGoal
166+  goal.withContext do
167+    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
168+    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
169+    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
170+    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
171+      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
172+      let subgoals ← if config.clear
173+        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
174+        else pure subgoals
175+      return subgoals.toList
176+    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
177+    else
178+      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
179+      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
180+      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
181+      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
182+      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
183+      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
184+      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
185+      let subgoals ← if config.clear
186+        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
187+        else pure subgoals
188+      return subgoals.toList
189+
190+/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
191+  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
192+  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
193+def evalInvAlt (goals : List CasesSubgoal) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
194+  match alt with
195+  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
196+    if let some goal := goals.find? (matchTag tag.getId $ ·.ctorName.getD default) then
197+      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal.mvarId]
198+    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
199+  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
200+    if !goals.isEmpty then
201+      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics ·.mvarId)
202+    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
203+  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
204+where
205+  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
206+    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
207+  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
208+    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
209+    unless goals.isEmpty do
210+      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
211+    return goal
212+  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
213+    let goalMsgs := goals.filterMap (.ofName <$> ·.ctorName)
214+    return if goals.isEmpty
215+      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
216+      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
217+
218+@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
219+public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
220+  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
221+    let config ← elabInversionConfig config
222+    let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
223+    if let some alts := alts? then
224+      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
225+      for alt in expandedAlts do
226+        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
227+        goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·.mvarId)
228+      unless goals.isEmpty do
229+        reportUnsolvedGoals $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
230+    replaceMainGoal $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
231+  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
232+where expandInvAlts
233+  | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
234+    args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
235+  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
236+
237+end Lean.Elab.Tactic
238+
239+end -- meta section
240+
241+namespace Tests
242+open Nat
243+
244+set_option autoImplicit false
245+set_option pp.proofs true
246+set_option pp.fieldNotation false
247+
248+inductive IsZero : Nat → Prop where
249+  | iszero : IsZero 0
250+
251+example (n : Nat) (isz : IsZero n) : n = 0 := by
252+  inversion isz; rfl
253+
254+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
255+  -- cases le /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
256+  inversion leq; assumption
257+
258+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
259+  inversion +clear leq; assumption
260+
261+/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/
262+#guard_msgs(error) in
263+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
264+  inversion +clear leq
265+  guard_hyp leq
266+
267+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
268+  inversion leq with
269+  | refl heq eq =>
270+    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
271+    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
272+    assumption
273+
274+/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
275+#guard_msgs(warning) in
276+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
277+  inversion leq with
278+  | refl e _ | step k _ e _ =>
279+    try rw [← eq]
280+    sorry
281+
282+/-- error: Invalid wildcard alternative: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
283+#guard_msgs(error) in
284+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
285+  inversion +clear leq with
286+  | refl e | step k _ e =>
287+    try rw [← e]
288+    sorry
289+  | _ => sorry
290+
291+/-- error: Invalid alternative name `step`: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
292+#guard_msgs(error) in
293+example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
294+  inversion +clear leq with
295+  | _ e | step k _ e =>
296+    try rw [← e]
297+    sorry
298+
299+example (n m o : Nat) : [n, m] = [o, o] → [n] = [m] := by
300+  intro h
301+  inversion h; rfl
302+
303+inductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
304+  | nostutter0: NoStutter []
305+  | nostutter1 n : NoStutter (n::[])
306+  | nostutter2 a b r (hneq : a ≠ b) (h : NoStutter (b::r)) : NoStutter (a::b::r)
307+
308+example : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
309+  intro contra
310+  inversion contra with | _ contra =>
311+  inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
312+  apply h
313+  rfl
314+
315+inductive Vec α : Nat → Type where
316+  | nil : Vec α 0
317+  | cons {n} : α → Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)
318+
319+example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : ∃ hd tl, v = Vec.cons hd tl := by
320+  inversion v with
321+  | cons hd tl => exists hd, tl
322+
323+inductive Wec α : Nat → Type where
324+  | nil : Wec α 0
325+  | cons {n} (f : Nat → Nat) : α → Wec α n → Wec α (f n)
326+
327+/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
328+#guard_msgs(warning) in
329+example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Wec α (succ n)) :
330+    ∃ hd tl, v = Wec.cons succ hd tl := by
331+  inversion v with
332+  | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>
333+    guard_hyp eq : succ n = f m
334+    guard_hyp heq : v ≍ Wec.cons f hd tl
335+    sorry
336+
337+example (H : Bool → Nat → False) (n : Nat) : False := by
338+  apply H at n; apply n; exact true
339+
340+inductive EmptyRelation : Nat → Nat → Prop where
341+
342+example n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by
343+  intro contra; inversion contra
344+
345+example (n : Nat) : Nat := by
346+  inversion n with
347+  | zero => exact zero
348+  | succ n' => exact n'
349+
350+inductive silly : Nat → Prop where
351+| silly1 n (h : n > 1) : silly n
352+| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n
353+| silly3 n (h : exists m, n = m + 2) : silly n
354+
355+example {n} (h : silly n) : n ≠ 1 := by
356+  inversion h <;> omega
357+
358+inductive The : ∀ {α}, α → Prop where
359+  | mk : The zero
360+
361+example (h : The 0) : True := by
362+  inversion h with
363+  | mk => exact ⟨⟩
364+
365+lemma doubleNegation : ∀ P, P → ¬ ¬ P := by
366+  intro P p np; exact (np p)
367+
368+end Tests

33 -- # Typeclasses
44 
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6--- variable with no constraint on it:
5+-- So far we have discussed **parametric polymorphism**, where in Lean we can
6+-- declare a type variable
77 
88 variable (α : Type)
99 
10--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
12---     lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13---
14---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15---
16---     Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?
17-
18--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
19---     Yes, in Poly!
20-
21--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
22--- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
23--- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
24--- `a : α`.
25-
26--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
27--- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
28--- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
29--- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
30--- languages, such as traits in Rust.
31-
32--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
33-
34--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
35--- occurs in a list:
36-
37-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
38-  match xs with
39-  | [] => false
40-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
43-
44-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
45-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
46-
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
48-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
49-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
50-
51--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
52--- `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a type
53--- variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
54-
55-sf_expect_failure
56-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
57-    match xs with
58-    | [] => false
59-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
60-
61--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on a
62--- value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one way
63--- to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test to use.
64-
65-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
66-  match xs with
67-  | [] => false
68-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
69-
70-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
71-
72--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
73--- supply, the right equality function.
74-
75--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
76--- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify
77--- something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the needed
78--- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
79--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class, different ones for
80--- different types, are called *instances*. For functions that would use such
81--- instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on the
82--- polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This directs
83--- Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill in the
84--- appropriate instance when the function is called.
85-
86--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
87-
88-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
89-  match xs with
90-  | [] => false
91-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
92-
93-theorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
94-
95-theorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
96-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
97-
98-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
99-
100--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
101--- differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter `eq`,
102--- whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The
103--- instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at
104--- call sites for the particular type `α` that is used. Second, whereas
105--- `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to test equality,
106--- `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when we first used it,
107--- `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
108--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function `Nat.beq`
109--- explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in automatically based on
110--- the type `Nat` of the `List`.
111-
112--- Note to developers (xhalo32):
113---     This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes from
114---     `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of
115---     `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
116---     how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
117-
118--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the instance
119--- implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was fully generic —
120--- so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and
121--- no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
122-
123--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far. We'll
124--- see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how to define
125--- a typeclass in the first place.
126-
127--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
128-
129--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of our
130--- own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis — that made
131--- `==` resolve automatically above.
132-
133--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
134--- defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
135--- `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default value
136--- an explicit parameter:
137-
138-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
139-  match xs with
140-  | [] => defaultValue
141-  | hd :: _ => hd
142-
143-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
144-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
145-
146--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an element
147--- of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based on the type
148--- of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
149-
150--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things. One
151--- is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the caller
152--- always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some information about
153--- what it should search *for*.
154-
155--- Considering the second problem first: The way to provide this information
156--- is to *name* the type-level concept we're after — the **default value** of
157--- a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give
158--- a type-level concept a name; structures can also bundle together more than
159--- one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we only need a
160--- single field here.
161-
162--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
163---     "type-level concept" doesn't say much to me here, and structures are
164---     *not* type-level things. (Well, `structure`s are, but *a* structure
165---     satisfying some `structure` declaration is not, if you see what I
166---     mean...)
167-
168--- Considering the first problem: we need to mark this particular structure as
169--- one Lean should search for automatically — not every `structure`-typed
170--- argument should be.
171-
172--- Let's build up to what wewant in two steps: first the naming, as a plain
173--- `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the
174--- structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
175--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
176-
177-namespace DefaultValueScratch
178-
179-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
180-  value : α
181-
182--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to serve as
183--- the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is, by supplying
184--- a `Nat` for the `value` field:
185-
186-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
187-  value := 1
188-
189-example : natDefault.value = 1 := rfl
190-
191-end DefaultValueScratch
192-
193--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
194---     Maybe the example is not needed?
195-
196--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the sort
197--- of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs to for
198--- `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class`
199--- in place of `structure`:
200-
201-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
202-  value : α
203-
204--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of `def`, we
205--- use `instance`:

10+-- without any further information about the details of the type `α`. Here we

16+-- This is somewhat limiting, as we cannot inspect or non-trivially use any
17+-- particular `a : α`. What we might want in some situations rather than `α`
18+-- being completely generic is to partially specify its behavior. In Lean,
19+-- this happens through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called
20+-- **typeclasses**. This concept originated in the Haskell programming
21+-- language, and is analogous to features you may be familiar with in other
22+-- languages such as traits in Rust.

24+-- ## First Example: Inhabited Types
25+
26+-- Suppose we wanted to specify that a type has at least one inhabitant —
27+-- i.e., that it is not empty. We have previously seen `structure`, which
28+-- would allow us to express this as
29+
30+structure HasOneStruct (α : Type) where
31+  one : α
32+
33+-- As discussed previously, a structure is just an inductive type that comes
34+-- with a single constructor, in this case `HasOneStruct.mk`, along with a few
35+-- different syntaxes for convenience:
36+
37+def nat_hasOneStruct_mk : HasOneStruct Nat := HasOneStruct.mk 1
38+
39+def nat_hasOneStruct_brace : HasOneStruct Nat := {one := 1}
40+
41+def nat_hasOneStruct_where : HasOneStruct Nat where
42+  one := 1
43+
44+def nat_hasOneStruct_anonymous : HasOneStruct Nat := ⟨1⟩
45+
46+-- All of these are the same value, a structure of type `HasOneStruct Nat`
47+-- that we can thing of as carrying a piece of data (a term that is not a
48+-- proposition), the number `1`, as evidence that this type is not empty. We
49+-- can use this in proofs such as
50+
51+theorem nat_hasOneStruct_eq_one : nat_hasOneStruct_mk.one = 1 := rfl
52+
53+-- to see how this structure provably contains the value that we have placed
54+-- within it. In Lean, typeclasses work very similarly, and in fact are
55+-- implemented as structures. The only difference in defining a typeclass is
56+-- that we instead use the `class` keyword:
57+
58+class HasOne (α : Type) where
59+  one : α
60+
61+-- While the definition is essentially the same, including the constructor
62+-- `HasOne.mk`, the usage of typeclasses is different, and what allows us to
63+-- use them to express ad hoc polymorphism. Instead of using `def` to define
64+-- inhabitants of this type, we will instead use the `instance` keyword:
65+
66+-- Note to developers:

70+--     that what we're looking for in the infoview is the presence of this

74+  one := 1

76+-- The definition is exactly the same as above (and any of the alternative

79+-- **typeclass synthesis** or **typeclass inference**. To help see this, let's
80+-- define another instance of `HasOne` for `Int`, the type of integers ... -2,
81+-- -1, 0, 1, 2, ...
82+
83+instance instHasOneInt : HasOne Int where
84+  one := -1
85+

89+-- you can write

91+example : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
92+example : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
93+

97+example : instHasOneNat.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
98+example : instHasOneInt.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl

103+-- example looking at

218+def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
219+  match xs with
220+  | [] => false
221+  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl

223+unseal List.elem_nat in
224+theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
225+
226+unseal List.elem_nat in
227+theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
228+    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
229+

284+-- that mentions a typeclass `BEq`. Perhaps a better question is what exactly
285+-- the `==` notation meant in our original `List.elem_nat`. Let's look at a
286+-- usage of this notation with natural numbers, but turn off notation:
287+
288+set_option pp.notation false in
289+#check 1 == 2
290+
291+-- This may be a bit surprising, as you may have been expecting to see
292+-- `Nat.beq`, the function for boolean equality on natural numbers. What we
293+-- instead find is that `==` is a notation for the typeclass `BEq`:
294+
295+-- class BEq (α : Type u) where
296+--   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
297+--   beq : α → α → Bool
298+
299+-- What is happening in the background when we use the `a == b` notation is
300+-- that Lean is searching for an *instance* of the `BEq` typeclasses that
301+-- applies for `Nat`. An example of such an instance would be
302+
303+instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
304+  beq := Nat.beq
305+
306+-- where we are specifying that the usage of `==` for natural numbers should
307+-- correspond to the expected `Nat.beq`. So in order to write a function that
308+-- uses the notation for boolean equality over a generic type, we need a way
309+-- to express that there is some instance for `BEq α`. This is done using
310+-- **instance implicits**, where we place a desired typeclass assumption in
311+-- square brackets. Our corrected definition is then
312+
313+@[irreducible]
314+def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
315+  match xs with
316+  | [] => false
317+  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
318+
319+unseal List.elem_poly in
320+theorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
321+
322+unseal List.elem_poly in
323+theorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
324+    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
325+
326+-- where Lean can now infer the usage of `==` is the one that we have
327+-- provided.
328+

438--- proofs that use maps.

437+-- Here we have made use of the the fact that the type `TotalMap` is defined
438+-- as a function type, so technically Lean let's us use a function application
439+-- to get an element. While this is possible, it goes against the spirit we
440+-- have seen in previous chapters of defining interfaces to our types, like
441+-- characterizing lemmas. We would like that the public interface we design
442+-- for TotalMap to be independent of the fact that the definition is `α → β`.
443+
444+-- In the ideal, we should be able to substitute in a different type with
445+-- similar behavior without needing to change the public interface. Suppose,
446+-- just for the sake of argument, that we wanted to define total maps as
447+-- `List (α × β)` or `Std.HashMap α β`. Neither of these are functions, so the
448+-- syntax `∅ 1` wouldn't work. If this is the public interface to access
449+-- elements, it restricts the definition ot `TotalMap`, forcing it to be a
450+-- function of some kind.
451+
452+-- To abstract away the function application, we introduce notation for
453+-- accessing elements using square brackets. This let's us write `∅[1]` or
454+-- `m[a]` regardless of the underlying definition of `TotalMap`.
455+
456+-- We'll call the typeclass `MyGetElem`. The typeclass takes three type
457+-- parameters: the collection, the keys that can be used to index and the
458+-- elements that it returns. For example, let's say we have declared an
459+-- instance `MyGetElem (List Bool) Nat Bool`. One can think of the instance as
460+-- saying that *indexing into `xs : List Bool` with an index `i : Nat` returns
461+-- a `Bool`*. The notation we introduce for this is:
462+-- `xs[i] = MyGetElem.getElem xs i`.
463+
464+-- Don't worry about what `outParam Type` means, it's like a normal type
465+-- paramater with a hint to Lean that helps typeclass inference. The
466+-- `macro_rules` and the `app_unexpander` are minor technicalities for getting
467+-- the syntax to work.
527468 
528469 class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
529470   getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem

519+-- #### Updating
520+
521+-- More interesting is the map-updating function, which (as always) takes a
522+-- map `m`, a key `a`, and a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to
523+-- `b` and takes every other key to whatever `m` does. The novelty here is
524+-- that we achieve this effect by wrapping a new function around the old one.
637525 
638526 def update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β :=
639527   fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
640528

643531 -- like the desired map.
